city.xh.exh.east.4: «The Town Through the Eyes of Class 3B». Children's drawings: a tower, a gull, the ceiling like a big white palm. Under one, a crooked caption: "This is mum in the kitchen." Mum is drawn very large and very warm.
city.xh.exh.east.5: «The Permanent Collection». The seasonal shows have gone to storage, and the caretaker's favourite pictures remain. No captions: they hang, so they are needed.
city.xh.exh.north.1: «Three Shores». A lighthouse, a calm sea, dunes. There is not one wave in the calm sea: the painter forgot. But it is the warmest picture in the row.
city.xh.exh.north.2: The label has been changed: "The same three shores, seen from the water." The pictures hang as before, but the caretaker lowered them two fingers so you look as if from a boat.
city.xh.exh.north.3: A shelf of shells and amber has been added under the pictures: "What the sea gave back." The amber is real, the shells too, and one stone with a hole the caretaker calls "the eye".
city.xh.exh.north.4: Children's-view week: beside the lighthouse a child's drawing is pinned where the lighthouse smiles. Adults are embarrassed, but the drawing stays.
city.xh.exh.north.5: The three shores have hung for a long time and hurry nobody. The carpet under them is a little worn: so people look at them, and for long.
city.xh.exh.west.1: «Where People Go». Tourist posters of the sixties: a train, a palm, a mountain. A slip is stuck beside them: "The farthest place in this hall is this poster. The rest is nearby."
city.xh.exh.west.2: «Storm». The only noisy spot in the hall: in the painting the waves hit a pier. They say that in rain the sound really does join the picture, though it is of course the vault.
city.xh.exh.west.3: The posters have been swapped for bills of the amateur theatre's old plays: "A Wedding at the Lighthouse", "The Gulls Are Not Flying Home", "Three Sisters and a Neighbour". Admission was always free.
city.xh.exh.west.4: «School Journeys» week: maps with pins where the classes went. The farthest was class 6A: to the pier and back, overnight.
city.xh.exh.west.5: On the west wall hang posters nobody remembers any more. The caretaker says: "If nobody remembers, they are safest right here."
city.xh.ghost.day.1: A bare bulb on a thin stand at the edge of the stage. By day it is hardly noticeable, but a small plate beside it says: "Do not switch off. Not a whim, a tradition."
city.xh.ghost.day.2: The caretaker says that while the lamp burns, the stage is not empty. Who exactly is on it, he does not say.
city.xh.ghost.night.1: The only light in the dark hall. The bulb lights half a metre of floor and the plate with its name: "On duty". It is on duty always, even when nobody else is.
city.xh.ghost.night.2: In the dark hall the ghost light throws the shadow of its stand up the vaults, huge as a mast. Old actors say: while it burns, the ghosts rehearse and leave the living alone.
city.xh.ghost.prompt: E — look at the ghost light
city.xh.ghost.rain: Rain drums on the vaults and the ghost light seems to listen: the flame trembles a little in time. The caretaker says the lamp is merrier in the rain.
city.xh.ghost.snow: Snow muffles all the sounds of the hall and the lamp shines as if in wool. It is so quiet you can hear its filament warm up.
city.xh.guest.1: The guest book lies open. The first entry on the page: "Good. Only the echo repeated my sneeze twice." Signed: "A lover of quiet."
city.xh.guest.10: A fresh entry in a tidy hand: "The poster for next week is out: choir, lecture, dancing, and the theatre is reading a new play. We pin the evenings' ticket stubs on the board in the foyer. Come for the stubs." Signed: "The caretaker".
city.xh.guest.11: Underneath in pencil, in a hurry: "Please have pies by seven. The choir is hungry, and the choir only has a voice after a pie." And lower in another hand: "Pies from four. Do not rush the cook, he is rushing already."
city.xh.guest.2: "Sang in the choir, sang well. The choir leader said, 'Nearly.' That is the highest praise." Beside it, in another hand: "Confirmed."
city.xh.guest.3: "Danced until eleven. My shoes fell like heroes. Please compensate." Below: "We cannot compensate, but we will give you a pie."
city.xh.guest.4: In a child's hand: "I like the ceiling. It is like a big white palm. If I were a pigeon I would live here."
city.xh.guest.5: "The reading of the play about clocks went well. The director cried because she was laughing, or the other way round." Signed: "The handyman, a.k.a. the Clockmaker."
city.xh.guest.6: "Remark: the buffet ran out of pies at 19:10. Suggestion: bake more pies. Or start the evenings later." The signature is illegible, but heartfelt.
city.xh.guest.7: A note between the pages: "Who found the chess clock with the crack? It is not a prop, the club is looking for it." A pencilled reply: "Found. On stage, among the props. Will be returned soon."
city.xh.guest.8: "Premiere! We laughed, we clapped, the echo clapped with us. The applause lasted three minutes, two of them echo."
city.xh.guest.9: The last entry, on a clean line: "Come again tomorrow. Write your name here, we have left room." The room is really left, and a pen hangs on its chain.
city.xh.guest.prompt: E — leaf through the guest book
city.xh.lecture.idle.1: The hall is empty. The lecture is on Tuesdays at seven. A notebook of diagrams is left on the front row: a parabola, rays, a note "check in the left corner".
city.xh.lecture.idle.2: You sit right by the stage and the silence sounds as if someone has just left. On Tuesdays at seven they talk about the echo here. They say it is best heard from the front row.
city.xh.lecture.prompt: E — listen to the lecture from the front row
city.xh.lecture.title: The lecture
city.xh.lecture.tue.1: The acoustic engineer claps his hands and everyone waits. The echo comes back after a second and a half. "That is the vaults," he says. "They listen a little longer than we do." The hall applauds, and the echo applauds afterwards.
city.xh.lecture.tue.2: On the board a parabola, rays and arrows. The engineer explains why a whisper from the right corner can be heard in the left. I check: it can. The neighbour on my right pretends he said nothing.
city.xh.lecture.tue.3: At the end the lecturer asks everyone to say "Vaults" together. The sound comes back like a wave and goosebumps run down my back. "That," he says, "is acoustics. The rest is formulas."
city.xh.lights.day.1: A panel with six switches and handwritten labels: "Work light", "Footlights", "Spots left", "Spots right", "Curtain", "Do not switch on". By day there is little to click, it is bright anyway.
city.xh.lights.day.2: Click, and a pair of spotlights comes on over the stage. Click, and it goes out. The windows are high, the day is stronger, and the spots only turn faintly yellow, like birthday candles at noon.
city.xh.lights.eve.1: In the evening the panel comes alive: "Footlights", and the stage turns gold. "Spots left", and the piano gleams. "Spots right", and the mosaic shows on the wall. Only the "Do not switch on" stays untouched.
city.xh.lights.eve.2: Click-click-click: blue, red, white again. A lone stool on stage in the blue light looks as though it is about to sing.
city.xh.lights.night.1: Only "Standby" is on. The other switches stand in a row like piano keys. None may be touched until morning, the caretaker said.
city.xh.lights.sat.1: The premiere's lighting: "Footlights" at half, "Spots" on cue, blue for the lighthouse scene. A slip on the panel: "Don't forget: in the finale, light on the clock."
city.xh.makeup.day.1: A make-up mirror with bulbs round the frame, most of them blown. In it you are without make-up: ordinary, serious, slightly surprised. While no one is looking, you can pull a face.
city.xh.makeup.day.2: On the table, pots of greasepaint, a powder puff, and boxes labelled "Beard, light" and "Beard, heavy". There is also a nose. Just one, on elastic.
city.xh.makeup.eve.1: The make-up woman draws wrinkles with a pencil. The actor is eighteen and the part is seventy. "Don't breathe," she says, "or the age will run."
city.xh.makeup.eve.2: In the mirror it is no longer you but somebody's grandfather. The eyes are yours, though, and so are the thoughts. Let us hope the grandfather does not let you down.
city.xh.makeup.night.1: At night the mirror is dark, one bulb smouldering. In it another bulb is reflected, the ghost light from the hall. They look at each other and do not blink.
city.xh.makeup.prompt: E — look in the make-up mirror
city.xh.makeup.sat.1: Before the premiere everyone in the mirror looks alike: pale, bright-lipped, whispering their lines. The make-up woman says: "Spit three times over the left shoulder and forget." Someone spits. Someone forgets.
city.xh.mirror.1: A mirror along the wall, a barre before it, polished by palms to a golden shine. In the mirror you are a little taller than in life. Posture, probably.
city.xh.mirror.2: You try three waltz steps in front of the mirror. On the third, the reflection takes one step more. It has clearly been practising longer.
city.xh.mirror.3: A sticker on the frame: "Keep your back straight. Smile if you like. Breathing is compulsory." The last is underlined twice.
city.xh.mirror.4: In the corner of the mirror, the print of a small palm, and at waist height a larger one. It looks as if people here learn to dance from childhood.
city.xh.mixer.day.1: The sound desk under a cover made of an old curtain. The faders are labelled in pencil: "Choir", "Piano", "Microphone", "Do not touch!!!" The last label is the most worn.
city.xh.mixer.day.2: A reel-to-reel recorder. A note on its lid: "Recording of Wednesday's choir rehearsal. Listen after nine in the evening, it sounds better."
city.xh.mixer.eve.1: The amateur sound man nudges a fader and out of the speakers on stage comes the rustle of the hall. Then the fader creeps back and the hall becomes a little quieter, a little farther, a little kinder.
city.xh.mixer.eve.2: The tape clicks into a pause, and the whole hall hears someone tuning the piano on stage. One note, then another. The A turns out to be the most honest of them.
city.xh.mixer.night.1: The desk is under its cover and the lamp is off. Only a red light on the recorder blinks, as if listening to something.
city.xh.mixer.prompt: E — go up to the sound desk
city.xh.mixer.rain: On the tape it rains too: from the choir's Wednesday rehearsal, when it poured outside. The sound man says this rain is better than the real one because you can rewind it.
city.xh.mixer.sat.1: The desk on Saturday evening: the faders are up, the lamp is on, the sound man sits straight as at an exam. On a slip of paper: "First bell 18:55. Second 19:00. Third: as circumstances allow."
city.xh.mixer.sat.2: A big sheet lies by the desk: "Echo: do not damp, it is in the company. Clocks: do not forget. Applause: do not interrupt." The last is written bigger than the rest.
city.xh.pies.1: Little pies cool on the rack, golden, with a crack. The cook slaps a hand as you reach: "Blow first, then eat. A pie is like an echo: it does not come at once."
city.xh.pies.2: Pies with cabbage and with apple, you can only tell by biting. The cook counts: "Twenty-four. Six for the choir, ten for the dancers, the rest for the caretaker and you."
city.xh.pies.closed: The rack is empty, only crumbs on it and a note: "Pies from four to nine. If late, eat an imaginary one, it has no calories."
city.xh.pies.prompt: E — take a pie from the rack
city.xh.premiere.prompt: E — watch the stage from the house
city.xh.prog.fest: It is a holiday: in pencil on the poster is added "tea for all and dancing until the last waltz". The caretaker wrote below: "And no spare shoes needed, for the occasion."
city.xh.prog.fri: Friday, 19:00: a dance night in the side hall, with the buffet. A record plays, and with luck a pianist. Dancing until 23:00; a change of shoes is welcome.
city.xh.prog.lantern: Lantern Night: the poster has a lantern with a face drawn on it. A caption: "After the evening we do not put the hall lights out, the lamp waits until everyone has gone out with lanterns. Entry with a light is free."
city.xh.prog.mon: The Vaults' programme. Monday: no evenings. The hall rests, the caretaker wipes the banisters and scolds the draught. The buffet is open and there are pies.
city.xh.prog.newyear: New Year poster: a garland hangs on a treble clef. "A children's matinee in the morning, a grown-ups' one in the evening. A pie in between. The pie, by the way, is more important."
city.xh.prog.prompt: E — read the programme of evenings
city.xh.prog.sat: Saturday, 19:00: PREMIERE of Time, Forward!, the Wave theatre. Free entry, seats by affection. Dancing after the show.
city.xh.prog.sea: Sea Festival: the poster is in blue washes. "The choir sings about water, the lecture is about the echo over water, the dancing is to the waves. Wet shoes do not matter, but the carpet does not like them."
city.xh.prog.sun: Sunday, 14:00 to 19:00: tea dances for those who like to be home early. Children under twelve free, and welcome until the last waltz.
city.xh.prog.thu: Thursday, 18:00: the Wave amateur theatre rehearses the play Time, Forward! Spectators welcome; remarks accepted in writing, and afterwards.
city.xh.prog.tue: Tuesday, 19:00: a lecture, "Why the echo in the Vaults runs late". Given by an acoustics engineer, free entry. Please do not clap until the end: the echo claps for you.
city.xh.prog.wed: Wednesday, 17:00: the Surf choir, open rehearsal. You may sit in the hall and keep quiet. Singing along is allowed in a whisper only: the choir leader's condition.
city.xh.prompter.line.1: The prompter's stand at the left wing. A thick notebook lies on the slanted board: the play «Time, Forward!», every page scribbled over in pencil.
city.xh.prompter.line.2: The prompter's lamp with a green shade. Under it a pencil on a string and a note: "Read quietly. The echo repeats everything."
city.xh.prompter.prompt: E — open the play on the prompter's stand
city.xh.props.1: The props table: a telephone with no cord, a globe with the Pacific painted over the Baltic, an inkwell of dried ink. All so that a play about time looks like a play about time.
city.xh.props.2: In a box, a chess clock with a crack on the left dial. The tag: "Prop, act one. Return to the club when asked. If asked, we will. If not, we will anyway."
city.xh.props.3: A handwritten script of Time, Forward! with notes in the margins: "Pause here." "A longer pause here." "Pause, and light, please."
city.xh.props.4: An alarm clock with one hand. The director says the second hand is the audience: at the right moment it works out for itself that time is up.
city.xh.props.5: Under the table a crate marked "Echo (do not rattle)": inside, sheets of tin and two spoons. This is how the play sounds the Vaults' echo when the real one is late.
city.xh.rehearsal.fri: Dress rehearsal: costumes and lights. The dance in the side hall goes ahead; please do not come on stage in dancing shoes, and do not dance in the Mayor's scene.
city.xh.rehearsal.mon: A notice from the Wave theatre: "Parts are cast. Clockmaker: the handyman (he agreed, but only until nine in the evening). Mayor: the pie seller. Postwoman: the girl from the box office. Echo and Second Echo: twin brothers, they talk to each other anyway."
city.xh.rehearsal.sat: Today at 19:00, PREMIERE. Free entry, seats by affection. Please be nervous politely, shout "bravo" if you like, applaud as you see fit: the echo will back you up.
city.xh.rehearsal.sun: Thank you to everyone who came! The hall applauded longer than the play ran. Photos in the foyer, comments in the book. The next production is by request; apply to the handyman, he knows where the clock is.
city.xh.rehearsal.thu: Urgent! We need a big clock for act one, preferably a working one. Bring it backstage. No need to phone: the echo will hear.
city.xh.rehearsal.tue: The read-through is done. The echo in the Vaults sent every line back late, and the director decided it is even better: a third actor.
city.xh.rehearsal.wed: A request to the cast: the choir rehearses until 19:00, then the stage is yours. The Clockmaker must not die on stage before then: the hall is singing a lullaby.
city.xh.script.1:
TIME, FORWARD!
A comedy in three acts for the «Wave» theatre.
Characters: the Watchmaker, who keeps a workshop on the square. The Mayor. The Postwoman. A Chorus of Clocks (offstage).
In the margin: "Prompter! Read quietly. The echo in the Vaults repeats everything, you included."
city.xh.script.10: In red pencil under the notes: "Premiere on Saturday. Do not forget the key. Do not forget the Watchmaker. Do not forget that we are amateurs, which means we love it."
city.xh.script.2:
ACT ONE. The square of a small town. A clock on the tower never lies, because it does not run at all. The Watchmaker sits under it eating a sandwich.
WATCHMAKER. Twenty years I have mended other people's time. I never have time to mend my own.
city.xh.script.3:
MAYOR (enters without a glance at the clock). Am I late again?
WATCHMAKER. You are never late, Mr Mayor. We have nothing to be late by.
MAYOR. Then why do I feel I am running all the time?
In the margin: "Pause here. Let the house sigh."
city.xh.script.4:
POSTWOMAN (with her bag). A letter for the tower. No address. Only: "To whoever winds it."
WATCHMAKER. What is inside?
POSTWOMAN. I do not open them. But it ticks.
CHORUS (offstage). Tick-tock.
In the margin, heavily: "The chorus does not come in before the word 'ticks'!"
city.xh.script.5:
ACT TWO. The Mayor wants to stop the clock so that nobody hurries any more: an order, a stamp, a speech. The clock strikes thirteen.
MAYOR. Thirteen? There is no such hour!
WATCHMAKER. There is now. One extra hour, and it is yours.
Lights: slowly to warm. Do not damp the echo.
city.xh.script.6:
POSTWOMAN (reads the letter aloud). "Dear Watchmaker! By the time you read this I will no longer be able to wait. Wind the clock yourself, not by order. Your mother."
The Watchmaker is silent. The Mayor takes off his hat.
Director: "If someone coughs in the house, we hold the pause until they stop."
city.xh.script.7:
ACT THREE. The Watchmaker climbs the tower. Below, everyone waits. He puts in a key (a prop one, from the case in the foyer) and turns it. Nothing. Again.
WATCHMAKER. It is simple. You only have to want time to move forward. The rest it does itself.
city.xh.script.8:
The clock starts. Quietly at first, then louder, then the chorus takes it up. The square dances a waltz (if we manage to learn it: see Friday in the side room).
MAYOR. Good heavens, how fast it goes!
WATCHMAKER. As it should.
Bow. Curtain. Lights up in the house.
On the last page in pencil: "Thank you all. The echo bows too."
city.xh.script.9: On the back of the last sheet, the director's notes: "1. The Watchmaker speaks fast and the clock runs slow: swap them. 2. The Postwoman does not cry, she holds it in: that is different. 3. The Mayor takes off his hat on the word 'mother', not before. 4. The chorus breathes together. 5. Do not fight the echo, use it."
city.xh.sheet.dance.1: A leaflet with the evening's programme: a waltz, a polka, a foxtrot, another waltz (by request), the ladies' choice at the end. In pencil beside it: "Foxtrot only for those who are not afraid."
city.xh.sheet.dance.2: The music of the polka «Merry Feet». Over the third line, a drawing of shoes with little wings. Written: "Play faster than seems sensible."
city.xh.sheet.prompt: E — pick up the sheet music
city.xh.sheet.stage.1: Sheet music for the piano: the «Vaults» waltz, composed by a local music teacher. In the margin in pencil: "The left hand like steps across an empty hall. The right like an echo in no hurry."
city.xh.sheet.stage.2: The last bar is crossed out and rewritten: a fermata instead of a full stop. A note: "Hold until the caretaker coughs. If he does not cough, until morning."
city.xh.show.sat_day.1: The day run before the premiere. The hall is empty, and on stage everyone is in costume and terribly serious. The director sits in row five repeating: "Just breathe. The vault will say the rest."
city.xh.show.sat_day.2: The actors come out for a bow in front of the empty hall. They bow awkwardly, on a count. Then one of them sticks her tongue out at the echo. The echo, of course, does the same.
city.xh.show.sat_late.1: The play ended long ago. On stage only the ghost light, and the clock ticking quietly, the big one. It was left on stage. It is going.
city.xh.show.sat_show.1: The lights go down. From the wings comes the handyman in a waistcoat with a chain, surveys the hall as sternly as a clock showing the exact time, and says: "Time... goes on." The hall laughs, the echo laughs a little later.
city.xh.show.sat_show.2: Act two: the Mayor tries to stop the clock and it strikes thirteen. The Mayor is horrified, the hall delighted. Up in the gallery someone whispers, "That is not in the script." The prop master, presumably.
city.xh.show.sat_show.3: The finale. The Clockmaker winds the big clock and it goes. The light slowly warms. Someone on stage forgets a line, the prompter whispers, and the whole hall takes it up in a whisper. Applause for three minutes, two of them echo.
city.xh.show.wk_day.1: A rehearsal without costumes, in whatever they came in. An actor in a sweater plays the Mayor, an actress in a coat the town clock. The director takes off her glasses: "Very convincing. Only louder."
city.xh.show.wk_day.2: They are trying the lights on stage. A spotlight comes on, goes off, and each time someone says, "There you go." It is the most expressive line of the day.
city.xh.show.wk_eve.1: An evening rehearsal: the Clockmaker recalls his monologue, getting half way. The prompter whispers; the Clockmaker answers, "I know, I'm thinking." The director writes in her notebook: "Keep the pause."
city.xh.show.wk_eve.2: The choir sings something quiet behind the scenes while the postwoman's scene plays on stage. It turns out strangely beautiful: a letter read to a lullaby.
city.xh.show.wk_late.1: At night one ghost light burns on stage. The hall is empty, and the emptiness under the vaults seems a very attentive listener.
city.xh.soup.1: Soup in a big pot, a ladle the size of a scoop. The cook pours a bowl "for thanks" and adds a spoonful of sour cream: "That is not in the recipe, that is from the heart."
city.xh.soup.2: The soup today is vegetable, almost without meat, but with dill. The cook says: "The choir sings better on vegetable. Meat is heavy, it pulls the voice down."
city.xh.soup.closed: The pot is empty and washed for now. On the lid in chalk: "Soup from twelve to four. Sniffing is free at any time."
city.xh.soup.prompt: E — ask for a bowl of soup
city.xh.steps.after.1: The marks on the floor are painted, red for left and yellow for right. Enough steps for today: my feet ask for tea and quiet.
city.xh.steps.closed.1: The steps on the floor are painted: red for the left foot, yellow for the right. Practice on Fridays and Saturdays from seven in the evening, when the record goes on.
city.xh.steps.draw.1: Three steps clean, three crooked. The dance teacher says: "A draw. Half a waltz is yours already." And shows which half.
city.xh.steps.keys: E — step when the mark reaches your foot
city.xh.steps.lose.1: On the fourth step I trod on my own mark and got tangled. The red foot went left, the yellow right. The floor said nothing, but you could hear it sigh.
city.xh.steps.lose.2: Missed the mark and nearly sat on the floor. Someone laughs behind the mirror, kindly: everyone here has missed once, just earlier.
city.xh.steps.prompt: E — practise the steps on the marks
city.xh.steps.title: Steps on the marks
city.xh.steps.win.1: Six steps in a row and not one off the mark. Red foot, yellow foot, red. Someone in the corner says, "That is a floor that remembers you." The floor does seem to answer.
city.xh.steps.win.2: The box step came out clean: forward, side, together. The dance teacher claps: "The count has stuck by itself. That is the most important thing." My feet are still dancing a little on their own.
city.xh.tea.1: The samovar hums like a little steamer. You put the cup under the tap, the steam tickles your nose. Beside it sugar in a jar, and on the jar "No more than two."
city.xh.tea.2: Strong tea from a tin with an elephant on it. Fingers have long rubbed the elephant away, only the trunk is left. The trunk knows its business.
city.xh.tea.closed: The samovar is cold for now, with cones and kindling under it. A note on the wall: "Tea from three until closing. Before three, no tea, only tap water."
city.xh.tea.prompt: E — pour tea from the samovar
city.xh.text.booklet.title: The Vaults hall programme
city.xh.text.guestbook.title: The Vaults guest book
city.xh.text.script.title: «Time, Forward!»: the prompter's copy
city.xh.text.sheet_dance.title: Music on the upright: the dance programme
city.xh.text.sheet_stage.title: Music on the grand piano: the «Vaults» waltz
city.xk.1_crossword.1: Under the glass hangs yesterday's crossword, solved in pencil. The hand is even, the letters square, like a draughtsman's.
city.xk.1_crossword.2: A note beside it: "Right answers on Fridays. Wrong ones every day."
city.xk.1_crossword.3: Less than half is filled in. But "wind" is written in ink, so firmly that the author seems to be arguing with the printer.
city.xk.1_crossword.4: Six more words today. During the night, probably: the seller came to a shut kiosk and the crossword was already different.
city.xk.1_crossword.5: The seller has seen the solver: "Someone who waits for the last bus. In no hurry, knows everything except one word."
city.xk.1_crossword.6: One clue is left: "Eight letters: what a bus stop has most of." The pencil on its string waits on the bench.
city.xk.1_crossword.7: The seller whispers: "He sat on the bench till morning, thinking. They say you're quick. Take a look: there's a paper and a pencil."
city.xk.1_pencil.1: On the bench lies a paper with the crossword and a pencil stub on a string. Nobody is solving: the bus isn't coming and the squares are few.
city.xk.1_pencil.2: I solved a short one: "wind." It fit. My handwriting is worse, but confident.
city.xk.1_pencil.3: Thinking about the last clue: "what a bus stop has most of." "Buses"? No, there are hardly any. "Benches"? No.
city.xk.1_pencil.4: I sat, looked at the timetable, the clock, the road. The word kept turning but wouldn't fit the squares.
city.xk.1_pencil.5: I wrote it in: P-A-T-I-E-N-C-E. Eight squares, and every crossing fit. I put the pencil down and heard someone in the kiosk say quietly: "At last."
city.xk.1_phone.1: I dialled my own number, which doesn't exist here yet. Polite silence picked up.
city.xk.1_phone.2: I rang the information line: "What do you know about the weather?" "Everything except tomorrow." I hung up pleased.
city.xk.1_phone.3: The evening tone is softer than the day's. I dialled the number from the stop's notice: engaged. That is an answer too.
city.xk.1_phone.4: At night the payphone hums alone. I dialled the speaking clock: "Twenty-three fifty-nine," said a voice, and added: "Go to bed."
city.xk.1_phone.5: At the weekend you can hear farther down the line: somebody across town is laughing and doesn't pick up.
city.xk.1_wall.l1: The paper on the stand, under glass: today's issue, already with nose prints on it.
city.xk.1_wall.p1: LEADER. "A bus stop is the place where the town stops hurrying for a minute and starts reading." Editorial board: the newspaper seller and one pigeon.
city.xk.1_wall.p2a: TOWN LIFE. Yesterday the pier held an exhibition of fishing rods. The winner caught nothing, but hung beautifully.
city.xk.1_wall.p2b: TOWN LIFE. An unclaimed suitcase was found on the cable car. Inside: just a second mitten and a sandwich with a note, "Warm since morning."
city.xk.1_wall.p2c: TOWN LIFE. Schoolchildren are collecting stamps from every kiosk: the "Bus-stop passport." Grown-ups may join too, with ice cream.
city.xk.1_wall.p3a: WEATHER. Rain, says the forecast. Let it remember first what it came for.
city.xk.1_wall.p3b: WEATHER. Clear. The editors advise leaving the house without an umbrella and coming back without one.
city.xk.1_wall.p3c: WEATHER. Overcast with sunny spells in conversation. Tomorrow's forecast will be in tomorrow's issue.
city.xk.1_wall.prompt: E — read the paper on the stand
city.xk.1_wall.title: The wall paper by the kiosk
city.xk.2_bell.1: I rang. Someone looked out of the hatch, saw there was no rain, and smiled anyway: "All right. A scoop at half price, for persistence."
city.xk.2_bell.2: The bell chimed thin, like a spoon on a glass. A hand held a cone through the hatch: "This is for you. Cheaper only in daydreams."
city.xk.2_bell.3: A morning chime. "You're the first today," said the hatch. "The first gets a cherry. No cherries, so here's a double smile."
city.xk.2_cone.1: On the pole a waffle cone with three scoops: pink, white and yellow. The top one has slipped a little and holds on out of stubbornness.
city.xk.2_cone.2: A slip of paper is taped to the pole in a child's hand: "I want two scoops. Mum said when I grow up. I've grown 2 cm."
city.xk.2_cone.3: Under it a reply: "Until you grow another 3 cm, one. But I'm trying very hard not to notice."
city.xk.2_cone.4: The slip is smoothed out and boxed in a frame: "Grown." A tick beside it and a note: "Checked with a tape measure."
city.xk.2_cone.5: Each morning a sparrow sits by the pole waiting for a dropped wafer. It's already called Plombir. It doesn't mind.
city.xk.2_cone.6: A new line on the slip: "Two scoops for whoever rings the bell on the hatch first." Ringing is allowed.
city.xk.2_crate.1: A lemonade crate: hard to sit on and very good. From here you see the queue, so you see how business goes.
city.xk.2_crate.2: Hot: in the awning's shade the crate seems the coolest spot in town. A puddle from a melted cone is growing next to it.
city.xk.2_crate.3: Rain drums on the awning and it is dry beneath. The seller passes a napkin through the hatch without being asked.
city.xk.2_crate.4: The crate still holds the day's warmth. The freezer behind the wall hums a quiet lullaby.
city.xk.2_flavours.1: In chalk on the board: "Today: plombir, crème brûlée, plombir with jam. No chocolate; it was eaten at the weekend."
city.xk.2_flavours.2: Added: "Two scoops are allowed, but don't make a fuss." The scoops are drawn as circles; one is winking.
city.xk.2_flavours.3: "Weekend: chocolate! Two scoops for the price of one and a half. The queue is on the far side of the rubbed-out chalk."
city.xk.2_flavours.4: At the bottom, in a child's hand: "Is there ice cream with a mood?" Below, in an adult's: "There is. With a good one, any kind."
city.xk.2_flavours.5: Early on the board: "Ice cream before noon is not weakness but privilege."
city.xk.2_fountain.1: The fountain water smells of iron and summer. The jet leaps higher if you press with two fingers.
city.xk.2_fountain.2: In the evening the fountain gurgles lower. The water is lukewarm, as though it, too, had been left out in the sun.
city.xk.2_thermo.1: A street thermometer with big figures. The seller sets her range by it: under ten, only plain ice cream; over twenty, everything.
city.xk.2_thermo.2: The column is high: by the mark in red felt-tip, "cones going well." So is the queue.
city.xk.2_thermo.3: The column has crept to the bottom. In blue beside it: "Come anyway. We'll be glad; the ice cream won't be."
city.xk.2_thermo.4: Drizzle. The column sits on an even mark and the seller reads a book, with a piece of card under it in case of drops.
city.xk.2_thermo.5: At night the column stands like a sentry. On the card below, in chalk: "Goodnight, summer."
city.xk.3_chair.1: A chair with a cotton cushion: the owner keeps it for those who are too shy to ask for a seat.
city.xk.3_chair.2: At weekends old men sit here and discuss the timetable as if they were writing it.
city.xk.3_chair.3: Rain runs off the awning's edge exactly five centimetres from the knees. The owner says he worked it out.
city.xk.3_chair.4: In the evenings the cushion smells of pipe tobacco and apples. Someone has left a bitten one here.
city.xk.3_jar.1: A jar of matchboxes from the whole coast: "Yantar," "Lighthouse," "Summer '71." The lid is tight: looking is fine, opening is not.
city.xk.3_jar.2: A card: "Whoever quits brings a box. There are 31 in the jar. The 32nd is up to you, if you are one of those."
city.xk.3_jar.3: Now 33 boxes. One from a man who quit on Thursday, the other "just in case."
city.xk.3_jar.4: There are 36 in the jar. The seller admits that three are their own: "holidays, once a year. That doesn't count."
city.xk.3_jar.5: The jar is full. The seller counts the boxes and says: "Enough. This isn't a jar now, it's a testimony."
city.xk.3_lotto.1: A typed lottery sheet: numbers, sums, empty boxes. No winners are listed, but room has been left for them.
city.xk.3_lotto.2: Yesterday's draw: 4, 11, 17, 23, 31, 37. Somebody circled the thirty in red with three question marks.
city.xk.3_lotto.3: The draw: 2, 9, 14, 21, 28, 40. Written beside it: "All the sevens came up except the right ones."
city.xk.3_lotto.4: The draw: 6, 13, 19, 26, 33, 39. A signature underneath: "My birthday is the 26th. Checked."
city.xk.3_lotto.5: The draw: 1, 8, 15, 22, 29, 36. Every number seven apart. Someone wrote: "The calendar won."
city.xk.3_lotto.prompt: E — look at the draw sheet
city.xk.3_pipes.1: Six pipes on the rack: a cherrywood one, a chewed one, one carved with a gull. It smells of cherry and old polish.
city.xk.3_pipes.2: A plate: "Not for sale. Belongs to Grandfather T. and his grandfather. Looking is allowed, breathing on the varnish is not."
city.xk.3_pipes.3: A seventh pipe lies apart in a case. "Its owner hasn't smoked for three years," says the seller. "But he comes on Wednesdays and sniffs it."
city.xk.3_pipes.4: An old man stands by the kiosk sniffing an empty pipe. The seller pretends to count change.
city.xk.3_pipes.5: A note on the rack: "Thank you. Quit for real. I leave the pipe in the row." The seventh now stands next to the gull.
city.xk.3_weigh.1: The scales shuddered. A ticket: "Morning. Weight: slightly less than it seems. You are alert."
city.xk.3_weigh.2: A ticket: "Weight: reliable. Advice: ice cream is at the next kiosk; it weighs more than it seems."
city.xk.3_weigh.3: A ticket: "In the evening everyone is a little heavier. That's normal. That's the day."
city.xk.3_weigh.4: A ticket: "One doesn't weigh at night. But since you're standing here: the same weight, a thoughtful look."
city.xk.4_bench.1: A bench by the flower awning: the backrest is warm because a bucket and reels of ribbon lean against it.
city.xk.4_bench.2: In the morning the bench is damp and smells of the bucket water. You can sit: the florist lays down an old newspaper.
city.xk.4_bench.3: In the evening people wait for the bus here and end up choosing flowers. Many get off later holding what they came for.
city.xk.4_cal.1: The florist's calendar, winter: hyacinths in pots, fir twigs and whatever can be carried into a warm flat. The day the mimosa arrives is ringed in red.
city.xk.4_cal.2: The florist's calendar, spring: tulips for the Eighth of March, narcissi, then lilac. The lilac has "approximately" written by it, with two different pens.
city.xk.4_cal.3: The florist's calendar, summer: daisies, cornflowers, sunflowers on Saturdays. In the margin: "Do not sell the butterflies."
city.xk.4_cal.4: The florist's calendar, autumn: asters, chrysanthemums, sprigs of rowan. On the first of September: "Lots of white. Don't mix up with the hair bows."
city.xk.4_cal.5: A ribbon has been stuck to the calendar for the holiday. Beneath it: "Anything that blooms is a gift today."
city.xk.4_lilac.1: A note on the pink board: "Ales, buckets of lilac into the shade." "Please" is crossed out, above it: "PLEASE."
city.xk.4_lilac.2: A new note from Anait: "The lilac bloomed ahead of time. Don't blame it, it's in a hurry to live."
city.xk.4_lilac.3: Ales's reply: "I put it in the shade. But the lilac is hot anyway. That's how it is."
city.xk.4_lilac.4: Beside it a cross sunflower is drawn: "I want shade too." Someone signed under it: "You get the sun."
city.xk.4_lilac.5: Anait left Ales a sprig: "Smells like Mum when she was happy." The sprig has drooped, but the scent holds.
city.xk.4_lilac.6: On the back, a note for me: "If you come in the evening, water the sunflowers by the kiosk. Can on the left. Ales left early and they sulk without water."
city.xk.4_sniff.1: I put my nose to the nearest flowers: a bitter freshness, almost like after lessons when the windows are opened.
city.xk.4_sniff.2: After rain the chrysanthemums smell of earth and cold water. You want to stand and breathe until somebody calls.
city.xk.4_sniff.3: In the heat it smells of honey and warm dust. A bumblebee hums over the bucket and has no plans to leave.
city.xk.4_sniff.4: At night the flowers smell stronger than by day. Or it is simply quieter and so easier to notice.
city.xk.4_sniff.prompt: E — smell the flowers in the bucket
city.xk.4_watering.1: I watered the sunflowers by the kiosk with the can. They seemed to turn to me. Or to the sun. Or they were dizzy.
city.xk.4_watering.2: Evening watering is the right kind: the water doesn't evaporate, the flowers don't object. The can is empty, the buckets are full.
city.xk.4_watering.3: At night it's better not to touch the can: it clinks. But one sunflower got its water anyway.
city.xk.4_wrap.1: I held the kraft paper while the ribbon was tied. "A bow isn't decoration, it's a promise the bunch won't fall apart," I was told.
city.xk.4_wrap.2: I cut paper along a ruler. It came out crooked, but "crooked means by hand, and flowers like hands."
city.xk.4_wrap.3: I was trusted to tie three daisies and an ear of wheat. It came out like a first-grader's. "That's called tender."
city.xk.4_wrap.4: I tied the ribbon in a bow, then a double knot, then once more for luck. The bunch lasted all day. That's not my talent, that's the knot.
city.xk.5_chair.1: A steel chair by the departures stand: comfortable like a cabin seat, except that it does not sway.
city.xk.5_chair.2: In the morning those bound for Aton sit here. They read the same paper, but different pages.
city.xk.5_chair.3: At night from this chair you see a cabin cross the cable as a small light. In no hurry, like you.
city.xk.5_dep.1: The departures stand: on weekdays the cabins run often, for those on their way to work. Over the schedule a tiny red cardboard cabin.
city.xk.5_dep.2: Weekends: cabins run less often and slower. A note on the stand: "The view is paid for in time."
city.xk.5_dep.3: It is {time}. The stand promises: the last cabin leaves late, but the dispatcher asks you not to risk the last minute.
city.xk.5_dep.4: Fog: a red card on the stand, "Running with care." The cabins are fewer, but each carries more passengers.
city.xk.5_dep.5: Snow: "Cabins running. The bench keeps you warm. Don't forget your hat." The last words were added by someone's grandmother.
city.xk.5_dep.6: A festive stand: ribbons on every post. The cabins run with balloons at their windows.
city.xk.5_dep.prompt: E — look at the departures stand
city.xk.5_diagram.1: The diagram on the wall: the red line, Akademgorodok and Aton; the blue, Amber Shore and Zenith; the green, the Lighthouse. A dotted one is labelled: "Only in dreams so far."
city.xk.5_diagram.2: Beside it the arrow "You are here." It has been moved twice: first it was in the wrong place, then right, but nobody believed it.
city.xk.5_diagram.3: Someone has added a station by hand: "Bakery." It doesn't exist, but everyone rides there.
city.xk.5_diagram.4: A yellow line marks the one that only rumours run on. They say it has the loveliest view.
city.xk.5_fountain.1: The fountain water by the cable car smells of mountains, though there are none here. It must have dripped from the cabins.
city.xk.5_fountain.2: The night fountain babbles loudly, as if it wanted to be noticed.
city.xk.5_ledger.1: In the "Passengers' Questions" book I wrote: "Where do the cabins go at night?" I signed legibly so the answer could find me.
city.xk.5_ledger.2: I leafed through: "May I bring a dog?" "The dog will decide." "Why don't the cabins meet in the middle?" "You just blink."
city.xk.5_ledger.3: I wrote a question about the mitten. Right below, someone answered: "It isn't lost. It's on a business trip."
city.xk.5_ledger.prompt: E — write a question in the book
city.xk.5_lost.1: The case "Left in the cabins": a red mitten (one), a blue thermos, somebody's hat with a feather.
city.xk.5_lost.2: A tag on the mitten: "Cabin no. 7, Monday. Owner not found. Rides back and forth since Monday and seems to have learned the timetable."
city.xk.5_lost.3: A second mitten in the case! "Brought from cabin no. 3. A pair. Now we look for whoever lost both."
city.xk.5_lost.4: Both mittens are stitched together: "So they don't get lost again." No owner yet. The clerk keeps a request book.
city.xk.5_lost.5: A note in the case: "Owner found: a girl with a plait. She said she lost them on purpose so somebody would ride. Took them. The case is empty for the first time in a year."
city.xk.5_punch.1: The punch clinked. The ticket kept a hole shaped like a cabin. I wasn't going anywhere, but I kept the ticket.
city.xk.5_punch.2: I punched a ticket for an imaginary trip: "Stop: Zenith, 12 minutes, no changes." Nice when the route is short.
city.xk.5_punch.3: The hole came out slanted, like a cabin in the wind. An inspector would approve.
city.xk.6_clocks.1: The clocks on the board show different times, yet all of them are morning: the hands are stopped in different seconds of the same morning.
city.xk.6_clocks.2: The clocks show different things. The mender: "Each about its own. These about childhood, those about tomorrow."
city.xk.6_clocks.3: In the evening you can hear the clocks ticking out of step, like an orchestra whose conductor has gone to supper.
city.xk.6_keycut.1: The mender clamped a blank and said: "A key with no lock is just a metal hint." A minute later a new key lay on my palm. To what, he didn't say.
city.xk.6_keycut.2: The machine squealed and stopped. The key smells of hot metal. "For whatever you will need," said the mender, and was hardly joking.
city.xk.6_keycut.3: The key came out with wave-shaped teeth. "A rare pattern. It will fit doors that don't exist yet."
city.xk.6_keys.1: A board of keys on hooks. Each has a tag with a number and a word: "waiting," "not waiting," "gone but will be back."
city.xk.6_keys.2: A key tagged "The door not to be opened before Wednesday." It isn't Wednesday yet, so the key waits calmly.
city.xk.6_keys.3: A key without a tag but with a red thread. The repairer says: "The owner just doesn't like tags. I can see he will be back."
city.xk.6_keys.4: A key tagged "Lighthouse." The heaviest, hanging the lowest. No one has come for it yet.
city.xk.6_radios.1: Brisk morning exercises on the radio. The mender whispers: "This set doesn't need mending. It's like this only in the mornings, then it spoils."
city.xk.6_radios.2: A bulletin: "Wind north, sea calm, mood moderate."
city.xk.6_radios.3: A pioneer song crackles out of the set, as if through time.
city.xk.6_radios.4: An evening request concert. The request: "For the mender, from L." The mender pretends not to hear but mends more slowly.
city.xk.6_radios.5: The set hisses softly, catching something far off: an announcer in Norwegian, music, silence, the announcer again.
city.xk.6_shoes.1: On the rack, pairs without owners: a child's strapped sandal, a size-43 boot, one red bootee. Each waits for someone's feet.
city.xk.6_shoes.2: A tag on the red bootee: "Heels replaced, sole glued. Running allowed. Running away not."
city.xk.6_shoes.3: The size-43 boot is heavy and polished. The owner said: "I'll come after my shift." The shift was three weeks ago.
city.xk.6_stool.1: A stool for those whose watch has "just stopped." You sit until the repairer looks, the tick-tock behind the wall in place of music.
city.xk.6_stool.2: In the evening the stool is warm from the lamp behind the wall. A scratch on the seat looks like a clock hand: five to the hour.
city.xk.6_umb.1: A stand of umbrellas awaiting repair. Each has a tag: the black one "spoke," the blue "button," the yellow "temper."
city.xk.6_umb.2: Rain, and the stand has fewer umbrellas: the repairer has handed back three and taken the owners' word. The word needed no mending.
city.xk.6_umb.3: Snow: almost no umbrellas, but a small shovel has appeared with a tag, "beyond repair, but needed." It got taken too.
city.xk.6_umb.4: Clear: the umbrellas stand idle like people on leave. The repairer sorts spokes and hums.
city.xk.6_umb.prompt: E — look over the umbrellas in the stand
city.xk.6_watch.1: On a velvet pad lies a pocket watch. It ticks loudly, slightly unevenly, like a heart after running.
city.xk.6_watch.2: The lid is engraved "L. from L." The mender: "Brought in March, wanted for May. Mended by May. May has passed."
city.xk.6_watch.3: Each morning the mender winds it and puts it back. "So it doesn't get bored. Idle watches spoil first."
city.xk.6_watch.4: Inside the lid in tiny letters: "If found, return it. If not found, wind it." The mender didn't show me; I saw by chance.
city.xk.6_watch.5: Today the watch keeps exact time, second for second. "See? They waited. Now to wait for whoever comes for them."
city.xk._bin.1: In the bin: tickets, an ice-cream cup and a newspaper folded in four. Somebody didn't finish it.
city.xk._bin.2: A flyer sticks out of the bin: "Silence for rent. Cheap." Someone added: "Cheap, how cheap?"
city.xk._bin.3: In the morning the bin holds fresh wrappers and one whole loaf. The crows pretend it has nothing to do with them.
city.xk._bin.4: By day the bin fills before your eyes: sweet wrappers, lollipop sticks. A sparrow sits beside it, an expert in the field.
city.xk._bin.5: In the evening there is a glass of half-drunk tea beside the bin. Somebody left it for later.
city.xk._bin.6: At night the bin rings hollow if you drop a coin in. I didn't try.
city.xk.closed.1.1: The newspaper kiosk is closed: the rack is bare, yesterday's papers hang on a hook with a polite note, "Take them free."
city.xk.closed.1.2: The papers are tied up for the night with string. In the morning they will be laid out and the town will learn what happened.
city.xk.closed.2.1: The ice cream is under a lid for the night, a note on top: "Don't dream, it's rock solid anyway."
city.xk.closed.2.2: The awning's striped shadow over the hatch has gone out, and the queue of two sparrows has dispersed.
city.xk.closed.3.1: The tobacco kiosk is closed: the display is empty, only a matchbox stands on its edge like a watchman.
city.xk.closed.3.2: The hatch is papered over from inside. Through it you see only a bulb wrapped in cotton wool.
city.xk.closed.4.1: The flower kiosk is shut, the buckets moved under the awning, which makes there seem more flowers. A note: "Drink water. The flowers do too."
city.xk.closed.4.2: The paper roll on the bench is covered with a towel like a birdcage. The florist will come when it gets light.
city.xk.closed.5.1: The ticket kiosk is closed: a diagram on the glass with "You are here" pointing right at the shut hatch. Witty.
city.xk.closed.5.2: The booth is closed but the cabins still run: the light over the cable creeps from station to station as ever.
city.xk.closed.6.1: The workshop is shut: the clocks in the hatch each show their own time, and none is wrong, since nobody is in a hurry.
city.xk.closed.6.2: On the sign: "Gone to mend time. Back on time, but not yours." The keys on the board jingle in the draught.
city.xk.closed.counter.1: The kiosk is shut. A scrap on the hatch: "Open in the morning. Thanks for waiting."
city.xk.closed.counter.2: Silence behind the shutter. Only a cooling fridge ticks inside.
city.xk.closed.hatch.1: The hatch is shuttered and chalked: "Back when I'm back." Nothing happens meanwhile.
city.xk.closed.hatch.2: The shutter is down, the padlock hangs on its honour. It is dark behind the glass; only three glass jars gleam.
city.xk.coll.pass.title: Bus-stop passport
city.xk.k1notice.1: Torn from a notebook and pinned: "Lost: a pocket watch. Silver, engraved 'L. from L.' Finder gets tea and a talk. Ask at kiosk no. 6."
city.xk.k1notice.2: Under the notice, in another hand: "Saw something like it on the mender's tray. Running fast, as usual."
city.xk.k1notice.3: In the notice "lost" is crossed out and "forgotten" written above. Below: "Forgotten very long ago. L."
city.xk.nt.1: "A mitten found. A left one. Ask the kiosk keeper: he wears it on his lapel until the owner turns up."
city.xk.nt.2: A school project: "Bus-stop passport." It needs stamps from all six kiosks. The paper is with the group leader, the ink with the kiosk keepers.
city.xk.nt.3: A slip: "Wanted: a bicycle. Not too fast." The phone number has been torn off, all but the last digit.
city.xk.nt.4: Three people already have a full row of stamps in their passports. Someone added: "A fourth went back for the last one and forgot where it was."
city.xk.nt.5: A note: "Lost: a lampshade. Marks: yellow, likes the wind."
city.xk.nt.6: "The project was defended with top marks. Thanks to all six kiosks. Keep the stamps, they are prettier than the grade."
city.xk.nt.7: A ribbon runs over all the notices: it is a holiday. The bus keeps to its Sunday run.
city.xk.nt.8: The ink on the phone-number slips has run in the rain. Only the word "call" can be read.
city.xk.stamp.rain: In the rain the print comes out a little blurred, like a postmark on an old card. It looks better that way.
city.xk.stamp1.1: The "Newspaper" stamp: an open sheet with columns. The print comes out slightly slanted, as if rushing to make the issue.
city.xk.stamp1.2: In the morning the ink is fresh: even the small columns read, and the date prints bold.
city.xk.stamp1.3: In the dark the stamp goes down blind. A cloud-shaped blot stays on the paper, and it still counts.
city.xk.stamp2.1: The "Ice cream" stamp: a cone with three scoops. The ink smells of vanilla. Somebody must have mixed it in.
city.xk.stamp2.2: By day the stamp sticks to the fingers: the freezer is next to it and always drips something.
city.xk.stamp2.3: At night the cone prints upside down. The seller says that way it doesn't melt.
city.xk.stamp3.1: The "Matches" stamp: one matchbox filling the whole picture. The print is even; the fingers smell of sulphur and resin.
city.xk.stamp3.2: By day the kiosk is open and the stamp lies in plain view. It is heavy enough that the print never shifts.
city.xk.stamp3.3: In the evening the box prints paler: the ink dries toward night. Press a little harder and it shows.
city.xk.stamp4.1: The "Flower" stamp: a six-petal daisy. One petal always falls short; it is meant to.
city.xk.stamp4.2: In the morning there is a drop of dew on the stamp, and the print gleams until it dries.
city.xk.stamp4.3: In the evening the florist waters everything before closing, the stamp included. The print comes out damp.
city.xk.stamp5.1: The "Cabin" stamp: a red gondola on a cable. The ink is red, as the Akademgorodok-Aton line should have it.
city.xk.stamp5.2: At travel hours everybody stamps, and a little queue of gondolas builds up on the sheet.
city.xk.stamp5.3: At night the cabin prints against stars: the ink is dark blue. The dispatcher says that is the rule after nine.
city.xk.stamp6.1: The "Key" stamp: a brass key with three teeth. The print is so crisp you could unlock the paper with it.
city.xk.stamp6.2: By day the clocks tick in the booth and the stamp goes down in rhythm: tick, tick, print.
city.xk.stamp6.3: In the evening the repairer wipes the stamp with the watch cloth. After that the key on the print shines like a real one.
city.xk.tt.1: Weekday mornings: a bus every ten minutes. Someone has pencilled underneath: "Every twelve."
city.xk.tt.10: Pencilled at the bottom: "The driver, Lyova, waves. Wave back."
city.xk.tt.11: At the bottom in a child's hand: "The bus is drawn on the back." The back is stuck to the glass, so you have to take it on trust.
city.xk.tt.2: Weekdays, midday: a twenty-minute gap. Under the "Daytime" column in chalk: "Except lunch."
city.xk.tt.3: Weekday evenings: more often again. The stop smells of pies from somebody's bag.
city.xk.tt.4: Weekends: fewer buses, but every one carries somebody with a basket or a fishing rod.
city.xk.tt.5: It is {time}. No buses until morning; the timetable just keeps the place till the first run.
city.xk.tt.6: In the rain someone has written "+5 minutes" by the figures. Yesterday's figure has one too.
city.xk.tt.7: In snow the timetable is a wish. In the corner somebody drew a snowman holding a ticket.
city.xk.tt.8: On holidays the bus runs to the Sunday timetable. A scrap of paper stuck on the glass says so.
city.xk.tt.9: At the bottom a sticker: "Request stop. Raise your hand."
city.xpl.closed.any: A closed library is quiet. Everything stands in its place and is in no hurry.
city.xpl.closed.board: Monday, the library is closed. A card on the door: "We open on Tuesday at ten. The returns box works at any hour."
city.xpl.closed.counter: Nobody at the desk. A note with a tea-ring on it: "Tuesday from ten. Do not lose your reading diaries."
city.xpl.closed.shelf: On Mondays the shelves rest. The spines look straight ahead, and I do not disturb them.
city.xpl.diary.fri: Theme of the day: our town. Find the house you live in on the old map by the book wall. If you cannot, the house is newer than the map. That earns a stamp too.
city.xpl.diary.full: A new slip is pinned to the stand: "Diary completely filled? Then drop in on the librarian. She knows what to do with readers like you."
city.xpl.diary.half: At the bottom of the sheet, in pencil: "Eight stamps already. That is not a grade, it is a route."
city.xpl.diary.mon: Reading diary. Today is Monday and the pages are clean: it is the books' day off. Not laziness, just the order of things.
city.xpl.diary.sat: Theme of the day: anything at all. On Saturdays you may hop from shelf to shelf. At 11 a story is read in the children's corner.
city.xpl.diary.sun: Theme of the day: the sun. At 11 the Sunday story, and tea afterwards. Diaries are accepted for a stamp right up to closing time.
city.xpl.diary.thu: Theme of the day: poems. Reading aloud is allowed in a half-voice. Loud reading earns no stamp, but a good face does.
city.xpl.diary.tue: Theme of the day: the sea. Read a page on the Sea shelf, then get your stamp at the lending desk. On Tuesdays the kettle in the staff room is put on for two.
city.xpl.diary.wed: Theme of the day: birds. Find out from the field guide how a great tit differs from a blue tit, then go outside and check. A stamp for an honest check.
city.xpl.leave.1: I wrote one line on the postcard: "We are waiting here. The kettle is on every Tuesday." I slipped it between the ticket and the clock without numbers. From the pile by the shelf I took another one to keep: they always leave a few here.
city.xpl.leave.2: I did not sign it: he will know who it is from. I laid the postcard with the other bookmarks and held my palm on it as on a warm mug. From the pile I took a clean one to keep.
city.xpl.leave.3: The postcard got damp at the edges while I carried it under my jacket. I wrote anyway: "It rained. I came." I put it with the bookmarks to dry and took a dry one from the pile.
city.xpl.leave.4: In the evening there's nobody at the shelf. I chose my words for a long time and wrote only: "Till tomorrow." From the pile I took someone's card with a lighthouse.
city.xpl.leave.5: It's a holiday, and the pile is full of cards with flags and flowers. On mine I wrote "Happy holiday, whoever you are" and took one with fireworks.
city.xpl.leave.prompt: E — slip a postcard into the guide
city.xpl.ledger.1: The 1968 loan ledger, in a blue folder. Entry of 14 May: "Guide to Sundials, lent until 28 May. Reader: G. N." The due date is crossed out and written again, many times, in different inks.
city.xpl.ledger.2: At the bottom of the page, fresh ink: "Returned." Today's date. Below, a second hand: "Received. Do not worry. The kettle is hot."
city.xpl.ledger.3: A second entry in another hand: "Came on Tuesday. Did not come behind the desk, drank his tea standing by the window. Left before I turned round. Left a daisy."
city.xpl.ledger.4: A sheet is pinned to the ledger: "A messenger is needed. Somebody young, whom he will not be afraid of. Let them slip a postcard into the book, the rest is my business."
city.xpl.ledger.5: The ledger is closed, with a fresh line on the cover: "Reader: G. N. Status: comes on Tuesdays." Beside it, on a saucer, an empty cup and a daisy.
city.xpl.notice.1: The reading room is open from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m., except on Mondays. On Mondays the library rests: shelves need to breathe out now and then.
city.xpl.notice.10: Over the New Year days a tree made of books stands in the reading room. The top ones may be taken down only by two people, and only to be read.
city.xpl.notice.2: Please do not stack more than five books on the tables. A falling tower is not reading, it is gym class.
city.xpl.notice.3: Lost a scarf, a mitten or a thought? Scarves and mittens are in the box at the lending desk. Thoughts are harder, but we try.
city.xpl.notice.4: To the reader from 1968. Your loan card has turned up: no. 3-217, lovely handwriting, the surname blurred by time. The fine for all these years: zero roubles, zero kopecks. We counted twice.
city.xpl.notice.5: A small lamp has appeared by the Returned shelf. We did not put it there. Please leave it on: somebody finds it easier to read that way.
city.xpl.notice.6: A second bookmark was found in the Guide to Sundials: a drawn clock without numbers, only a shadow. Signed: "If it is cloudy I will come all the same." A spare lamp for cloudy days has been bought.
city.xpl.notice.7: To our young readers: one quiet story needs a messenger. Postcards are at the lending desk, four roubles. Slip one into the Guide on the shelf by the window. We expect a reply on Tuesdays, at tea time.
city.xpl.notice.8: On Tuesday both cups were empty. That is a good sign: it means they were drunk. The book has been lent to the reader again, due date: "when he has finished". Thank you, all messengers.
city.xpl.notice.9: There is a festival in town today. The lending desk closes at six: the librarian wants to go to the square too, and we are letting her.
city.xpl.piano.1: I lifted the lid two fingers' width and play as if the keys were cotton wool. From the next pod somebody tapped the wall softly: once, approvingly.
city.xpl.piano.2: I play very softly, a lesson in whispering. The pod answers with all its concrete and, oddly enough, it sounds beautiful.
city.xpl.piano.3: Evening, few readers. I played everything I remember. From the hall below somebody applauds: pages rustle, one by one, like small palms.
city.xpl.player.1: In the morning the children's record from Saturday is still on the player: "How the Little Bear Found a Trumpet". The librarian says it gets more plays than any symphony.
city.xpl.player.2: By evening the records in the box are muddled, and on the player an orchestra is playing something slow. I didn't change it: someone left it for whoever came next.
city.xpl.player.3: When it rains they put on the record of sea songs here. The needle hisses, and you can't tell where the recording ends and the window begins.
city.xpl.player.4: On the inner sleeve, in pencil: "Listen with your eyes closed. Tested. The periodicals desk."
city.xpl.pressA.fri: Friday: the weekend listings. An old film at Rassvet, a chess evening at the Cog club, a story for the smallest at the library. A note below: "Come with your parents, parents listen too."
city.xpl.pressA.mon: The bound run of the Town Herald for last week. There is no fresh issue: on Mondays the print shop rests together with the library.
city.xpl.pressA.sat: Saturday, the thick issue: a half-page crossword. Somebody has pencilled in "lighthouse" where "sea" was wanted, and it turns out both fit.
city.xpl.pressA.sun: The Sunday supplement, readers' letters. One begins: "I should like to find the person who borrowed a library book in May 1968 and took it away for a long while." Signed: "The Library."
city.xpl.pressA.thu: Thursday: an interview with the lighthouse keeper. Asked whether he gets bored, he answered: "I have people to talk to: thirty-three lamps, and all different."
city.xpl.pressA.tue: The Town Herald, Tuesday. On the front page the cable car, which has a new cabin again. Below in small print: the tide table and a yellow umbrella lost near the department store. A reward is promised to the finder.
city.xpl.pressA.wed: Wednesday: a report from the fishermen's pier on how to wean a gull off stealing from the tray. The editors' conclusion: you cannot. The recipe for pasties on page three is given without gulls.
city.xpl.pressB.fs: A chess magazine: a game played by post between two towns over four years. The last move was sent on a postcard. No winner is named: both insist they lost.
city.xpl.pressB.mt: The magazine Sky Above Us: a table of sunrises and sunsets for the week. One sunset is circled, with a note beside it: "The best one is the one you can see from the reading room."
city.xpl.pressB.su: A children's magazine: how to make an hourglass from two glasses and one patient week. Beside it, in somebody's pencil, a clock without numbers, only a shadow.
city.xpl.pressB.wt: Sky Above Us, an article on sundials: the shadow is shortest at noon, then stretches until it becomes night. The author calls it the most honest way to count time.
city.xpl.radio.1: In the morning the office radio mutters the exercises and the news. The librarian brews tea to the forecast and always says, "Wrong again, I bet."
city.xpl.radio.2: After lunch, a radio play. The librarian turns it down but not off, and in the quiet of the hall you can hear somebody in the play opening a door.
city.xpl.radio.3: In damp weather the radio picks up two stations at once: one is singing, the other reading the weather report. Together they make something truthful.
city.xpl.radio.4: There's a holiday concert on the radio, and for once the librarian turned it up. "Today it's allowed," she told the shelves.
city.xpl.returned.1: The Returned shelf: books with no loan slips and no readers, but with neat bookmarks. All the spines face the window as if waiting for weather.
city.xpl.returned.2: On top lies the Guide to Sundials, lent on 14 May 1968. The cover is worn soft. On the first page in pencil: "I read slowly. Forgive me."
city.xpl.returned.3: Between the pages is a cable-car ticket to the Lighthouse station. The date has rubbed off, but the stamp is the kind only people who treasure tickets have.
city.xpl.returned.4: A new bookmark: a clock without numbers, only the shadow of a gnomon. Signed: "If it is cloudy I will come all the same." I looked out of the window. The sky is just like that.
city.xpl.returned.5: On the shelf a card in the librarian's hand: "If you are reading this and have a postcard, slip it into the Guide. I will pass it on. Do not ask to whom: he will come himself."
city.xpl.returned.6: There are now three bookmarks in the Guide: the ticket, the clock without numbers and a daisy. The daisy is dry but does not crumble: it was carried carefully in a pocket.
city.xpl.returned.prompt: E — look at the Returned shelf
city.xpl.returned.rain: Rain. The lamp by the Returned shelf burns brighter than usual, and I see it is not here by chance: cloudy days are his days.
city.xpl.returns.1: The returns box. Its slot is exactly the thickness of a book: no thinner, no thicker. Inside it is muffled and warm, like a mailbox in winter.
city.xpl.returns.2: A card is stuck on the lid: "Books may be returned at any hour. We will not ask why it took so long."
city.xpl.returns.3: Under the slot there is a faint pencil mark on the metal: somebody checked whether a book would reach the bottom. It did.
city.xpl.returns.4: A corner of an envelope sticks out of the slot. Address: "The library, to the shelf by the window." I did not pull it out: it is not mine. But I can almost see the bookmark inside: a clock without numbers.
city.xpl.returns.5: The box is empty. That is news too: for the first time in many days nothing was returned and nothing was taken. The librarian says that happens when everything is in its place.
city.xpl.returns.6: On Monday the library is shut, but the box works round the clock. A corner of paper shows white in the slot: "To the reader from 1968. The kettle is on Tuesday, as usual. The librarian."
city.xpl.returns.prompt: E — look into the returns box
city.xpl.scope.1: The telescope stands at the pod's round window. Below: the terrace roofs, washing on lines and a strip of sea between two houses.
city.xpl.scope.2: I turned the telescope on the cable car. A cabin is creeping up, and somebody inside is reading a newspaper without looking out.
city.xpl.scope.3: At night there are only lights in the eyepiece: the lighthouse, a few windows, a lamp on the pier. The lighthouse blinks, as if checking everyone's still there.
city.xpl.scope.4: I caught the Moon in the telescope. It filled the whole lens, and you could see how bumpy it is. From far away it doesn't admit it.
city.xpl.scope.5: Fog. The eyepiece is full of white milk, and only now and then a roof floats up out of it and sinks again.
city.xpl.stamp.1: The librarian takes an ink pad from a drawer, breathes on the stamp and presses a round mark into my diary: a lamp with a green shade. "For quiet hours," she says.
city.xpl.stamp.2: At weekends the stamp is different: an open book with wings. "For reading with no use at all," the librarian explains. "The most valuable kind."
city.xpl.stamp.3: Four stamps in the diary. The librarian leafs through it and nods: "You can tell you are not reading for a grade."
city.xpl.stamp.4: Eight stamps, and the diary has swollen. She holds the cover down with a finger: "One day people will read it instead of you. Do not take offence, it is a compliment."
city.xpl.stamp.5: Twelve. The librarian takes out a red pencil and underlines my name on the cover: "This is not a mark, it is a bookmark."
city.xpl.stamp.6: The diary is full: a mark for every shelf, even the Returned. The librarian is silent for a long moment, then presses the last, big stamp: a clock without numbers. "I put that one in one reader's card. Long ago." Now you may come on a Tuesday for tea.
city.xpl.stamp.prompt: E — ask for a diary stamp
city.xpl.story.1: The librarian settles into the armchair by the round rug, and the little ones swoop down on the bean bags like sparrows on crumbs. Today's story is about a Little Lighthouse that was afraid of the dark. Every evening it lit its lamp so the ships would not be frightened, and the ships sailed off without saying thank you. But one day a small boat came back and blinked in reply. Since then the Lighthouse has not been afraid of the dark: it knows someone is sailing toward it in there.
city.xpl.story.2: A story about the Torn Page, which told everyone it came from the most important book. The page was picked up from the floor, smoothed out and held against another book. It fitted as if it belonged. It turns out that the right page sometimes simply gets lost on the way. The little ones argued for a long time about which book it came from. They agreed: a future one.
city.xpl.story.3: Today the story is about a Cat who lived in the reading room and followed those who had dropped a bookmark. He brought the bookmarks back in his teeth, carefully, by the corner. The readers thought that was how things were done. The Cat did not object. The children swore never to lose a bookmark again, just in case, so as not to teach the cat to work.
city.xpl.story.4: A Sunday story about the Kettle that boiled for two on Tuesdays. Once the one it boiled for was half an hour late, and the Kettle kept boiling all that time so the tea would not cool at once. The children listened very quietly. Then they asked whether the latecomer arrived. The librarian smiled: "You will tell me that when you grow up."
city.xpl.story.title: Story hour
city.xpl.tea.1: On Tuesdays the kettle is put on for two. The librarian nods at the second cup: "Have it. If he comes, I will pour again." The tea is strong and smells of thyme.
city.xpl.tea.2: The second cup is already warm: somebody was here before me. The librarian does not raise her head: "He asked me to say he got the postcard. And that our tea is too strong." I drink and stay quiet so as not to scare anyone off.
city.xpl.tea.prompt: E — take a cup of tea
city.xtx.art_grey_sea.1: Visitors think our sea is blue. It is grey, and that is the richest colour of all. In the morning it is silver, like the inside of a shell; at noon steel, with a green vein; before rain the colour of an old coin; after rain (my favourite) almost pink, because the sky above it hasn't decided what to do yet. I counted twelve greys and gave up: the thirteenth always overtakes.
city.xtx.art_grey_sea.2: How to paint the sun. Not at all. It cannot be painted; you can only paint what it does. Leave a white spot on the paper: that will be it. Then put beside it a warm shadow on a wall and a golden edge on the water. The viewer will finish it himself, and what the viewer has finished he loves more than what is served to him on a plate. I studied this for forty years and can say it in a minute. The minute can be spent on tea.
city.xtx.art_grey_sea.3: Advice for the young. For a lighthouse take the same paints as for a cloud: light and white are not different until a shadow is beside them. A good landscape is not one where everything is visible, but one where something is left for later. Paint the bench, but don't paint the person on it: let the viewer sit down himself. And don't throw away failed studies. On the back of one of mine lies a fish-soup recipe, on another a letter I never sent. That is painting too.
city.xtx.art_grey_sea.title: Twelve Greys: Notes of a Landscape Painter from the Upper Terrace
city.xtx.birds_coast.1: Gulls. The herring gull is the biggest, sixty centimetres. Its bill is yellow with a red spot, and it laughs as if it had just heard a good joke about you. The black-headed gull is smaller, thirty-eight. In summer its head is not black but chocolate; for winter it takes the hood off and keeps a dark smudge behind the ear. The common gull is the gentlest: no spot on the bill, a dark eye, a kind look. All three take bread, but the common gull asks politely.
city.xtx.birds_coast.2: The crow family. Rooks walk the lawns in flocks, and in their black tailcoats they look like the poor relations of an orchestra. The hooded crow is always alone and always busy. The jackdaw is smaller, with a silvery nape; its "chack" carries from every rooftop. The magpie builds a nest for every storm and sleeps in none of them. The raven is rare and enormous and says "kronk", as if dropping something heavy and valuable. If you think a crow is looking at you and counting, you are right.
city.xtx.birds_coast.3: The small ones. The great tit says "teacher, teacher"; the blue tit is slighter and brighter, as if painted in watercolour that hasn't dried yet. The goldfinch in its red mask counts thistle seeds. The bullfinch is pink-breasted and solemn, and sits on a rowan as if at a reception. The tree sparrow and the house sparrow look alike, but the tree sparrow has black spots on its cheeks, as if it had got dirty and won't admit it. At the feeder on the lower terrace the regulars are tits; sparrows arrive in a crowd and never leave in debt.
city.xtx.birds_coast.4: By the month. March: the starlings appear and the street sweepers say goodbye to their brooms. April: swallows at the jetty, the first sometimes alone and endlessly lonely. May: swifts; they never land, they only flash past and scream, and every rooftop gets a little brighter. August: the swifts vanish overnight. November: waxwings on the rowan, lovely as a postcard and greedy as children. Tick with a pencil, and in the "where" column be honest. The swan hisses in every season.
city.xtx.birds_coast.title: A Pocket Guide: Birds of the Promenade
city.xtx.chess_openings.1: Let us begin with the Italian Game: this is how decent people get acquainted. White puts a pawn in the centre and brings a bishop out onto the diagonal, as one holds out a hand. Black answers in kind. Both look at the f7 pawn, which is each side's weak spot, and each pretends to look by chance. Lev Markovich says the Italian teaches friendship: if you slap the hand away, it's your own fault, and if you shake it, you have a game for the whole evening.
city.xtx.chess_openings.2: The Sicilian Defence is a girl who was told, "Let's do it my way," and answered, "Let's do it our way," and went round by the side. Black does not repeat White's move but plays from the flank, and the game becomes sharp, noisy, with castling to opposite sides and shouting from the audience. Zoya plays nothing else. She says the Sicilian is never boring, and boring people don't play it. Here the author makes a pencil note: "Check. Vadim plays it."
city.xtx.chess_openings.3: The Spanish Game, or Ruy López, is a long tea. White's bishop aims at the knight that guards a pawn, and nothing happens for twenty moves. And then everything happens at once. Uncle Grisha loves it because you can think aloud and nobody interrupts. The book's last advice: "The opening exists to get you to the middle of the game alive. The rest is known to those who have played. And those who haven't should sit down and play. A game is better begun than postponed."
city.xtx.chess_openings.title: Chess Openings, Told to a Neighbour
city.xtx.cog_chess_ladder.1: The rules of the ladder. 1. You may play only someone no more than two rungs above you. 2. The winner swaps places with the loser and enters the game in the book, briefly, without excuses. 3. The loser stands the tea. Tea is served with sugar but without reproach. 4. Thursdays are blitz, any clock, as long as it ticks. 5. If a dispute cannot be settled, call Tamara Ilyinichna. She doesn't understand chess but she understands people, and in our club that is what matters.
city.xtx.cog_chess_ladder.2: No. 212. González vs Kask. Italian Game, drawn on move forty. Both pleased. Kask wrote: "He offered me a draw, I wanted to decline, but he looked at me in such a way that declining would have been rude." González added below: "I wanted to win. But tea is tastier than victory." Both stood the tea and nobody objected. The ladder stayed as it was, which in such cases counts as the best result.
city.xtx.cog_chess_ladder.3: No. 213. Nowak vs an unknown player. The stranger wore a club jacket too big for him and played Black. Nowak wrote simply: "Lost in twenty-eight moves. It was beautiful. He left without giving a name but left the queen on the table to be put away." Under the entry, a different hand: "It was me. I'll come Thursday." At the end of the book Tamara Ilyinichna pencilled an empty line and wrote: "For him."
city.xtx.cog_chess_ladder.p4_1: Today is Thursday, blitz. The clock belongs to the club, take care of it. Whoever finds the real one gets the right of the first move for the whole week. We play on any clock, as long as it ticks, but not on sand ones: sand, as we know, runs as it pleases. Sign-up with Tamara Ilyinichna until six in the evening, and after six with fate.
city.xtx.cog_chess_ladder.title: The Chess Club Ladder: the Book of Games
city.xtx.cog_model_manual.1: Section one: "What You Need at the Bench". A sheet of three-millimetre plywood, a fretsaw, sandpaper, glue, clothes pegs, a jar of water and patience. Put the patience in first; the rest can be borrowed if need be, but not that. Pin the drawing by the corners and never in the middle: the middle will be needed by the eyes. The bench rule: if in doubt, put the tool down and look at the part for a minute. Often the part will explain what it wants.
city.xtx.cog_model_manual.2: The motor launch, in three days. Day one: cut the frames. Don't hurry; one extra stroke of the saw costs an hour of correction. Day two: glue the keel and frames, hold them with pegs. The glue smells of apples, which is normal. Day three: cover with veneer and paint: red below, white deck, blue wheelhouse. Then the paint dries for a day, and this rule is not up for discussion. The impatient who touch it with a finger remain in the launch's history as a print, but we don't hold it against them.
city.xtx.cog_model_manual.3: The glider. The ribs are thin as splinters; break them without shame and cut new ones: a glider loves the patient, not the flawless. Cover the wing in tissue without a single wrinkle; a wrinkle is an air pocket. Spray it with water and the paper tightens like a drum. Make the first flight indoors, from a landing, into the draught rather than with it. It is good if after the first circle it settles on a bench. It is bad if on somebody's hat. It is very bad if the hat starts to chase it.
city.xtx.cog_model_manual.title: The Model-Maker's Manual (compiled by L. A., bound in sticky tape)
city.xtx.cog_photo_guide.1: Day one: negatives. We wind the film off in complete darkness, by touch, counting the turns in a whisper. The light must not be switched on, even if you are dying to see how it came out: film doesn't forgive curiosity. Developer, water, fixer, water again, all of it to a count. At the end a strip of small dark frames hangs on the line, in which the light is dark and the dark is light. You can get used to it, but it takes time.
city.xtx.cog_photo_guide.2: Day two: contact sheets. All the frames go on one sheet and come out small as postage stamps. Take a loupe and a red pencil: circle the best. Seryozha Gusev's rule: "If a frame is good at first glance, don't trust it, look a second time. If it's good the second time too, circle it once. If you circled it three times, you've fallen in love, and that's no longer a criterion." The choice is made quietly, alone, and explained afterwards.
city.xtx.cog_photo_guide.3: Day three: printing. The sheet under the enlarger, red light, and everyone whispers though the red light doesn't care. We count the exposure by the clock on the second bench: click the left button, click the right; at twelve we lift the frame. If you're not sure, make test strips: cover the sheet with card and uncover it in parts, each part two seconds longer. Then into the tray, and watch it emerge: first the horizon, then everything else, and last of all, what you took it for.
city.xtx.cog_photo_guide.4: Day four: drying. The prints hang on the line and drip, and the lab smells of vinegar. Gloss or matt paper, an eternal and unresolvable question; the club is split evenly, and both sides drink tea together. A dried print is lighter than it looked in the red light: allow for it when printing, or on day three you will overdo it. Sign on the back in soft pencil: the place, the hour and who was beside you. In a year this will turn out to be the main thing in the picture.
city.xtx.cog_photo_guide.p5_1: Today in the lab: negatives. Newcomers: look first, then get started. Don't switch the light on while the red lamp is lit on the door, and when it isn't, ask anyway, just in case. Wind the film by touch and in a whisper. Seryozha Gusev is on duty and will explain everything if you are not shy of asking, and there is nothing to be shy of.
city.xtx.cog_photo_guide.p5_2: Today in the lab: contact sheets. The loupe and red pencil are by the window; do not take them away.
