Dry the contact sheet flat, not on the line, or the frames will curl into a tube and look at each other. When choosing frames, remember the rule: circled twice means you already love it.
city.xtx.cog_photo_guide.p5_3: Today in the lab: printing. The clock is on the second bench; don't jostle it, it is nervous enough. At twelve we lift the frame, not at eleven and not at thirteen: thirteen counts here as character, eleven as haste. Don't mix up the trays: the left is developer, the right is fixer, and the middle is water and justice.
city.xtx.cog_photo_guide.p5_4: Today in the lab: drying. Don't touch the prints with wet fingers, however much you want to. They hang on the line by a corner, not by the face. It smells of vinegar until evening, and that is normal: it is how the lab lets you know work is going on. Those arguing about gloss and matt, please argue in whispers.
city.xtx.cog_photo_guide.title: Photo Circle Sheet: Four Days of One Photograph
city.xtx.cook_pie.1: Apple pie for a large tin. Six apples (sour ones, from a garden, not a shop: shop apples bake in silence), one and a half cups of flour, a glass of sugar, three eggs, a spoon of cinnamon. The batter is runny, like thick sour cream, and that is right: if it is stiff, you are building a house, not a pie. Apples go on the bottom, batter poured over. They will float up later; don't take offence.
city.xtx.cook_pie.2: Bake in an oven where a draught and a good mood live, forty minutes at medium heat. Don't open the door until it smells. The smell arrives at the thirty-fifth minute: first cinnamon, then sugar, then the home. If someone appears in the kitchen door and says, "What have you got in there?", consider the time up. Test with a matchstick, but don't eat the matchstick; it isn't in the recipe.
city.xtx.cook_pie.3: A pencil note on the last page: "On Sundays our terrace smells of pie because we all have the same notebook. The neighbour downstairs bakes the same one, only with walnuts, and we swap slices across the stairwell on a rope. I call the basket the cable car. The recipe isn't mine, it was passed down a chain. If you are reading this, you are in the chain. Bake it and pass it on."
city.xtx.cook_pie.title: Maria Zinovyevna's Kitchen Notebook: the Sunday Pie
city.xtx.eng_cable.1: First there was a path nobody walked in winter: concrete on the slope, ice on the concrete. The fishermen looked up and said, "Only a bird goes up there." Then an engineer took a tape measure, climbed to the topmost platform and simply unrolled it down the slope until the tape ran out. At the last mark he drew a pencil cross: "First station here." And so it turned out, to within a hand's breadth.
city.xtx.eng_cable.2: The hardest part turned out to be not the pylons but the rope. It was hauled in sections and spliced on site: twelve people, one night, and no word louder than a whisper, so as not to lose count of the strands. In the morning the rope lay on the pylons, sagged, tightened and suddenly rang in the wind, thin as a guitar. The brigade leader said, "So the road has got a voice." Ever since, in a strong westerly you can hear it sing, and the operators say it means good weather.
city.xtx.eng_cable.3: The first trial run was made without people: a sack of sand and a hat were put into the cabin so that it looked as if someone were riding. The sack arrived. The hat blew off at the third pylon, and they searched for it until evening. A boy from the lower terrace found it and received for it the first ticket, which he then carried in his pocket for years. The second run already had people, and an accordion played in the cabin, because silence was more frightening.
city.xtx.eng_cable.4: Now the line carries schoolchildren, fishermen, the post and people who need to think. The timetable hangs at every station, but the real timetable is this: the cabin arrives when you have stopped waiting. On the last page, by hand: "I built it so that people could climb more easily, and it turned out that it helps them come down calmly. I don't know which of the two matters more." The signature has worn away; only a flourish is left, shaped like a cable.
city.xtx.eng_cable.title: The Cable Car: a Site Foreman's Notes
city.xtx.garden_concrete.1: There is no soil on the terrace, but there are boxes. Take wooden ones, from fish; they are already salted and fear nothing. Pierce the bottom in five places: the water must leave, not live there. Bring soil from the lower road, a bucket at a time, and don't complain that it is heavy: it is the only part of the work that needs no decisions. Write the plant's name on the box. In a month you will have forgotten what you planted and will be glad of the hint.
city.xtx.garden_concrete.2: The wind. It is the master here and arguing is useless. Plant tall things on the lee side by the wall, put low ones in front. Geraniums like our air: they need only light, and they take salt as a compliment. Grow potatoes in a barrel: earth them up as they grow, and in autumn you will pull out more than you expected. Plant a sunflower by the southernmost wall: it will watch the Sun and turn, and the neighbours check the time of day by it.
city.xtx.garden_concrete.3: On patience. Everything here grows more slowly than in books. Radishes are in no hurry, dill thinks for a week, and tomatoes turn red exactly when you stop looking at them. The author advises against standing over the box: it slows things down. Water in the morning so the roots drink before the heat, and talk to the plants quietly, in passing, as neighbours do. They don't understand the words but they understand they haven't been forgotten.
city.xtx.garden_concrete.title: A Garden on Concrete: Boxes, Wind and Patience
city.xtx.kesha_phrasebook.1: How it began. Kesha came to us with the first coffee machine, in its box: the owner said the box was roomy, and so was the bird. For the first three weeks he was silent and watched with one eye. On the fourth he said, "Next stop, the Saucer." We jumped. Now I write down everything he says, because in this town that is the rule: if something happens twice, you start a notebook.
city.xtx.kesha_phrasebook.2: Vocabulary. "Next stop, the Saucer": in the morning, when you have just come in. "Mind the doors, please!": when someone heads for the stairs; there are no doors but everyone ducks. "Ticket": to whoever stands at the bar with empty hands. "Horizon": to nobody, just so, in the silence. "Terminus" is not from him but from us: say it, and he will answer, "Please vacate the cars." Or "Thank you for the ride", if he is in a good mood.
city.xtx.kesha_phrasebook.4: Feeding rules. Only sunflower seeds, and only after the word "Terminus". No bread, no sugar, no one else's bun, even if he looks like a beggar. Don't touch the seeds hidden under the perch: those are "till the next stop". Whoever feeds him by the rules gets a pastry from us, on the house. Kesha knows it and pretends not to, but whenever you come in, he is already looking at the door. Waiting.
city.xtx.kesha_phrasebook.p3_1: Observations, morning. In the mornings Kesha listens to the coffee machine and says nothing: he evidently likes the way it coughs. If at that time you say "good morning" to him, he turns away, but after a minute turns back. I consider that his way of saying "hello". By eight he comes to life, by ten he is already ordering the queue about.
city.xtx.kesha_phrasebook.p3_2: Observations, evening. Toward evening Kesha softens. If there are few people, he sits on his perch with his head tilted, listening to the jukebox. He likes "D-3"; when it is played he sways his head in time. If someone lingers by the window, Kesha says "Horizon", and the person starts as if remembered. Perhaps that is just what it is.
city.xtx.kesha_phrasebook.title: Kesha's Phrase Book (the barista's notebook, the cover dusted with seeds)
city.xtx.kids_lamp.1: At the very edge of the promenade stood a little lamp. By day it slept, and in the evening it lit up and shone three steps around: on a bench, a bin and a puddle. The lamp was kind but very much afraid of the night. "It is so big," it thought. "And I am so small. What if it doesn't notice me and swallows me?" So every evening it shone with all its might and trembled a little.
city.xtx.kids_lamp.2: One day the gull Klava landed on the lamp. She was coming back from the far shore and was tired. "Why are you trembling?" asked Klava. "I'm afraid of the night," the lamp admitted. Klava thought and said, "The night is not big, it is only long. And it is not alone, either. See, over there by the lighthouse? And up there on the hill? You all shine a little, and the night can see every one of you." The lamp looked and saw: it was true, lights were burning everywhere.
city.xtx.kids_lamp.3: Klava stayed with the lamp till morning. She told it about far shores where lamps stand in a row and talk by winking at each other. The lamp listened, and the night grew shorter. Then the sky at the edge of the sea turned white and then pink, and out of the water rose the Sun, big, warm and sleepy. "Hello," it said. "You shone well. Now you can rest." The lamp went out, but not from fear, rather like a person who has finished a task and breathed a sigh.
city.xtx.kids_lamp.4: From then on the lamp was not afraid. If it grew darker than usual in the evening, it glanced at its neighbours and winked: the little lights winked back. And Klava sometimes came to sit on its top. She said it had the best view of the sea and the calmest lamp in town. The lamp blushed with pleasure, and for a second its light turned a little pink. That is why, if you see a pink light on the promenade in the evening, don't be surprised: somebody has just been told a kind word.
city.xtx.kids_lamp.title: Klava the Gull and the Lamp That Was Afraid of Night
city.xtx.local_terraces.1: Before the terraces there was a village under the slope: twenty households, a smokehouse and a well whose water tasted of iron. The slope was thought to belong to nobody, and goats grazed on it. When the architects came, they did not cut the hill away but decided to be polite: to set steps on it, like a staircase down which the hill could quietly walk to the sea. The goats were told they were not being evicted but promoted.
city.xtx.local_terraces.2: There are six terraces, and each has its own character. The lowest smells of seaweed and fresh bread, and the early risers live there. The second is the school and clinic terrace, where someone is always running with a satchel or a thermometer. The third is for sport, with its tower and the cable car station. The fourth is severe, built of concrete boxes, but has the best view on a clear day. The fifth is quiet, the sanatorium's. As for the sixth, it was first designed as a lookout and then they changed their minds and left the sky.
city.xtx.local_terraces.3: They say a handprint was left on the first slab as it was cast: the foreman pressed his hand in for luck. The slab has long been under asphalt, but children still feel for it and find quite other things: a coin, a key, a button. Someone noticed that in this town everyone is looking for something and finds something else. That is perhaps the most exact definition of Lyudmilovsk, and it fits in one sentence, though the author worked on it for half a year.
city.xtx.local_terraces.4: The last chapter is called "What Is Left of the Village". The well is left: it has been closed with a grating, but in the mornings buckets of flowers are set by it. The smokehouse is left, now a workshop. The goats are left, or rather their descendants, and they still know how to find the steepest bit of slope and look down on the architects. "The town was not built," it says on the last page, "it arrived by itself. We only laid the steps."
city.xtx.local_terraces.title: Six Terraces: a Short History of the Town
city.xtx.medicine_home.1: On caution. This book is no substitute for a doctor. It substitutes only for panic, and only for the first twenty minutes. For a fever, for pain that doesn't pass, and for anything that truly worries you, go to the clinic: it is on the second terrace, and they expect you there even when they look busy. The rest of the book is about how to wait out an ordinary evening with a cold without losing your dignity.
city.xtx.medicine_home.2: A cold in the nose. Warm tea with honey, woollen socks and the window open a hand's breadth: air is needed too. A scarf doesn't cure, but pretends to, which is sometimes more important. It helps a great deal to sit by the window and count the gulls. If you counted more than twenty, you are no longer ill but out for a stroll with your eyes. Sleep as much as you are given. Choose a pillow on which every matter can be settled, and in the morning you needn't remember the decisions.
city.xtx.medicine_home.3: A separate chapter: "When You Are Simply Sad". There are no pills here. Go out to the nearest bridge and look at the water, or, if no water can be seen, at the sky. Talk to someone you don't have to explain anything to: a neighbour, a dog, whoever is sitting beside you on a bench. Eat something warm. By evening it won't be exactly cheerful, but it will be quieter. Quieter is also health. In the margin, in a doctor's hand: "Correct. Tested on myself."
city.xtx.medicine_home.title: The Family Home Doctor (sixth edition, corrected)
city.xtx.music_orchestra.1: The sanatorium orchestra met on Wednesdays in the former dining hall, which still smelled of stewed fruit. Nine players: four violins, a cello, a flute, a double bass that was moved on a trolley, and the conductor Eduard Karlovich, whose hands shook with age but whose beat did not. They tuned for a long time. Eduard Karlovich would say, "Gentlemen, we need one A. Only one. The rest we have."
city.xtx.music_orchestra.2: They had lost their tuning fork in a move, and took the note in different ways: from a piano that had been out of tune since before the war, or from the kettle. Once, in a calm, when the windows were full of the steady noise of the sea, Eduard Karlovich raised his hand and said, "Listen. That's it." And indeed: if you listen to the sea on a windless day, there lives in it a quiet, very low A, as if someone far away were holding a bow and not daring to begin.
city.xtx.music_orchestra.3: Ever since, before every concert the orchestra goes out onto the veranda and listens to the sea in silence for five minutes: then they are all tuned alike, because they are listening to the same thing. Eduard Karlovich no longer conducts, but on Wednesdays he comes and sits in the back row. On the last page is a staff line in pen: a single note, long, with a fermata. Under it: "For those who do not dare to begin. Begin."
city.xtx.music_orchestra.title: The Sanatorium Orchestra: the Story of One A
city.xtx.poetry_steps.1:
The Staircase

Forty steps to the bakery,
fifty to the window with the geranium.
Every morning somebody counts them,
and every evening they count him.
I climb without hurry, as if
explaining to my feet what it is all for.
You are at the top, let us say, not waiting.
But the door, just in case, is open.

From the author's note: written on the ninth landing of the second staircase, where a bench stands on purpose for those who count the steps and lose count. There is no shame in losing count here: everyone counts, and only the staircase remembers.
city.xtx.poetry_steps.2:
The Port

A gull has landed on a mooring post and watches
a man drinking tea out of a jar.
Both know: neither of them
will sail today, and perhaps not tomorrow.
If the wind turns toward evening,
she will leave first. He will stay
to feed what stays,
and count that, too, as a voyage.

From the author's note: the gull was called Klava, and she knows it. The man with the jar of tea was me, but that is unimportant: in his place could be anyone who looks at the water and puts off leaving till tomorrow.
city.xtx.poetry_steps.3:
September

The sun still holds us by the sleeve,
but weakly now, like a friend at the station.
I tell it: go, we will manage.
It answers: only as far as the corner.
And truly, there it is on the corner,
gilding the brick a little, and your shoulder,
and then the house hides it behind itself,
and the street grows up.

From the author's note: "as far as the corner" is the corner with the bakery on the lower terrace. The sun lingers there for exactly the minute it takes to say the main thing. I checked by my watch and still didn't manage.
city.xtx.poetry_steps.4:
In Place of an Afterword

I wrote this on steps that smell of rain,
on the back of a ticket, on a palm, on a newspaper edge.
If you come across a sheet without a signature
lying on a railing, take it.
It was left not because it was forgotten
but because it could not be carried further.
Carry it on.
What is light will arrive.

In pencil on the sheet, in another hand: "Found it on the railing by the station. Carrying it on. If it is yours, forgive me, it is now a little bit mine."
city.xtx.poetry_steps.title: Iraida Vald, "Poems Written on the Steps"
city.xtx.rassvet_dance_rules.1: Rules of the floor. 1. Indoor shoes, clean and smooth. The floor is polished on Fridays and is grateful for it. 2. We count aloud, because nobody counts silently. 3. You may look in the mirror but not admire yourself: the mirror gets tired. 4. Don't look at your feet. The feet know; if they don't, they are only shy. 5. If you tread on your partner, thank them, don't apologise. An apology is one more step, and we need to land on the beat.
city.xtx.rassvet_dance_rules.p2_1: Today is Tuesday, waltz. One-two-three, one-two-three: heavy on one, light on two and three, as if you stepped on a stair and then the stair slipped away. For beginners: somebody must lead. If both decide they are leading, you get an argument, not a waltz. The teacher claps her hands; so do you, young man: it isn't applause but a metronome.
city.xtx.rassvet_dance_rules.p2_2: Today is Wednesday, foxtrot. The steps are quick and slow: "slow-slow, quick-quick". Everyone's face is solemn as at an exam, because the foxtrot forgives mistakes only if you don't look at them. Your partner asks you not to look at your feet: look at his shoulder. In a week you will forget about the shoulder and simply walk. That is dancing. The rest is decoration.
city.xtx.rassvet_dance_rules.p2_3: Today is Thursday, slow dances. The light is dimmed, the record rustles. There is one step: sway right, sway left. The point is not the step but the breathing: the teacher walks between the couples and whispers "breathe". The couples sway in place as if the floor were drifting a little. Anyone who came without a partner today needn't dance with the mirror. There is always somebody near who has nobody either.
city.xtx.rassvet_dance_rules.p2_4: Today is Friday, polka. Hop, hop, step. The floor bounces along with you, the mirror trembles, and nobody wants to stop first. When the record ends, everybody goes on hopping for a second and then laughs. The teacher asks: softer knees, or the floor will complain. Today the floor is polished, and after class you are asked not to leave until it has dried. It too must have time to rest.
city.xtx.rassvet_dance_rules.p2_5: Today is Saturday, request evening. Whoever asks for a waltz gets a waltz, whoever asks for a foxtrot gets a foxtrot. A request is written on a slip and laid on the piano, signed or unsigned. If a request names something that isn't in the programme, the teacher plays it herself, with one finger, until somebody works out the rest. That is how last Saturday a waltz was born that the whole hall now knows, though nobody has the music.
city.xtx.rassvet_dance_rules.p2_6: There is no class today, the floor is resting. The records lie in their sleeves, the mirror looks into the empty hall and waits for Tuesday. The rules stay in force at weekends: don't look at your feet, count aloud, thank people for trodden toes. If you feel like dancing, nobody prevents you from taking three steps alone. The echo will answer and may make a remark.
city.xtx.rassvet_dance_rules.title: Dance Class Rules (pinned to the mirror frame)
city.xtx.rassvet_programme.1: From the projectionist. Reader, you hold a programme that I copy out by hand every week, because we have no printing press, but we do have ink and firm intentions. There are two shows a day: at three and at seven. The ticket is thirty roubles, which is not a price so much as a mark of attention. Please do not talk, rustle or crack sunflower seeds. Rustling offends me and the characters in the film, and they do hear it, believe me.
city.xtx.rassvet_programme.3: How to watch. Choose your seat by temperament. The fifth row is for those who like to hear everything: the sound gathers there like water in a hollow. The front row is for children and romantics: the screen hangs over you like the sky. The back seats are for those who came to think and brought the film along just in case. If the person next to you laughs where nobody else does, don't turn round. Most likely he sees what the rest have missed.
city.xtx.rassvet_programme.4: At the end of the programme, in small print, but I'll read it aloud. "If you have read this far, you read everything that hangs on the walls. We need such people. Tell the ticket-taker you are one of them and he will smile. If he does not smile, check whether you have a ticket in your hand. If you do, all is well: it's simply the sort of smile he has today." Signed: "The Management and the Projectionist, in one person, because the second post has been cut."
city.xtx.rassvet_programme.p2_1: Today, Monday. In the afternoon, "Holiday at My Own Expense": a comedy about a hat that ran away on the first day and showed a holidaymaker the whole town. In the evening, "The Man Who Waited for the Lighthouse": about an old fisherman who for forty years straightened his scarf and then did not know what to do with the morning. Don't be shy of laughing in the afternoon and crying in the evening: the hall is used to it. Today the box office takes only smiles and thirty roubles.
city.xtx.rassvet_programme.p2_2: Today, Tuesday. In the afternoon, "How Lyudmilovsk Was Built": a black-and-white newsreel with a girl foreman and a tape measure ordering grown men about, and a piano on the stairs at the end. In the evening, "The Last Cabin": the night shift, a glove forgotten in a cabin and two minutes of silence at a shut door. After seven the dance class is in the foyer: noise is allowed, but in time. You can hear it from the hall and it doesn't disturb.
city.xtx.rassvet_programme.p2_3: Today, Wednesday. In the afternoon, "The Sun Is Our Home": a popular-science film in which the rays run to Earth for eight minutes while the whole hall counts along with the announcer. At the end a sunflower and a sleepy cat, both turned toward the light. In the evening, "A Letter in a Bottle": a girl with a Swedish letter and a town in which everybody translates it in their own way. Please arrive before the bell, not together with it. The bell is touchy.
city.xtx.rassvet_programme.p2_4: Today, Thursday. In the afternoon, "Three Friends and a Watermelon": a summer comedy about three friends carrying one watermelon while they were expected yesterday. In the evening, "Silence on the Air": a radio amateur who spent three nights noting dots and dashes, and one word in reply. The radio corner is open today and the photo circle meets at six. After the evening show it is better to keep quiet: after "Silence" fewer words are needed than it seems.
city.xtx.rassvet_programme.p2_5: Today, Friday. In the afternoon, "The Yard Champion": a boy who trains against a house wall and in the bread queue, and a little girl with plaits who wins the final. In the evening, "Waltz on the Pier": a couple who can't get into step, and a lamp that goes out only with the music. After the evening show the buffet stays open another half hour. We recommend a pie and an unhurried talk about who managed what in the waltz.
city.xtx.rassvet_programme.p2_6: Today, Saturday. In the afternoon, "The Case of the Missing Gull": a children's detective story in which a herring, a cat and one evasive swan are questioned. In the evening, "The Projectionist": he loves every film but sees only a slice through the booth window. No break between shows; the break is in the buffet, where it's two curd tarts per person. The projectionist asks you not to look back at the booth during the film. He knows you will, but he asks.
city.xtx.rassvet_programme.p2_7: Today, Sunday. In the afternoon, "The Hedgehog's Cable-Car Adventures": a hedgehog carries an apple to a friend, and in the cabin ride a giraffe, an orchestra and a very serious snail. In the evening, "The Empty Street": an old silent film with a pianist and a man who keeps turning the wrong way. The front row today is for those who came with a hedgehog or without. Sunday menu at the buffet: tea and whatever is left from Saturday.
city.xtx.rassvet_programme.title: Programme of the House of Culture Rassvet (for the week, free, not to be taken away)
city.xtx.rassvet_radio_log.1: How to keep the log. Date, time by the wall clock, frequency, call sign, signal strength on a five-point scale and one word of your own. The word is optional, but without it the log turns into bookkeeping. The first entry in this notebook: "Strength 5, clean signal, the operator in Riga asks us to repeat the weather. We repeated it. He thanked us and said our rain is prettier." We didn't argue: our rain really is pretty.
city.xtx.rassvet_radio_log.2: Entry, evening. "Tallinn, strength 4. The amateur told us about a cat that sits on his transmitter, so the signal comes and goes. He asked us to send greetings to everyone sitting on something warm." We passed it on. Next, Arkhangelsk: the operator spelled out a card letter by letter and read our address. House of Culture Rassvet, radio corner. We hadn't expected a card and were delighted. We answered the same evening, and it is marked in red.
city.xtx.rassvet_radio_log.3: Entry, night. We don't know how to enter this one. "At night the air is wide as the sea. An announcer in a foreign language reads out numbers, someone answers in Morse, and between them something quite different beeps. Around three, at the very edge of the band, something flashed through the noise: '...hearing you, Lyudmilovsk.' It did not repeat. We noted the time, the frequency and the strength: one. We put a full stop, then a question mark, then a full stop again." Below, in another hand: "I heard it too. Don't tell anyone."
city.xtx.rassvet_radio_log.p4_1: Thursday: the radio corner is open, and in the evening the film "Silence on the Air". The radio amateurs gather in the buffet beforehand, headphones round their necks, arguing about aerials so loudly that it carries to the box office. Then they discuss whether anything in the film was wrong. There was, but they are happy. Please don't praise the film in front of Georgy Alexandrovich; afterwards he walks about for three days with the face of an operator.
city.xtx.rassvet_radio_log.p4_2: A note for those who come in just like that: don't touch the red-ink pen, it is for QSL cards. The left earphone squeaks; that is not a fault but a character. If you suddenly hear the word "Lyudmilovsk" on the air, don't be frightened and don't keep silent: press the button and answer, "I hear you." We will write down the rest.
city.xtx.rassvet_radio_log.title: Radio Corner Log: Short Wave
city.xtx.science_spoon.1: You will need: a teaspoon, a glass of water, a window and patience. Start with the spoon. Look into its rounded side: you are small there, upside down and very serious. Turn it over: now you are big, the right way up and slightly surprised. It is a mirror that cannot flatter but can change its mind. The author asks you not to show the result to anyone in a bad mood today, or to anyone after lunch.
city.xtx.science_spoon.2: Experiment two. Lower the spoon into the glass and look from the side: it has broken. In fact it is whole; light simply travels in water differently than in air, and tells you not how things are but how it got here. "Refraction" is a stern word with a homely meaning: whatever you see through something is a little bit untrue. Try it on a friend, through the glass. Warn them first, or they will take offence.
city.xtx.science_spoon.3: Experiment three, in good weather. Catch a sunbeam on the spoon and send it to the ceiling. It trembles with your pulse. If you sit still, the bright spot will begin to drift across the ceiling by itself: it is not the spot, it is the Earth turning under us while we do not notice. Mark with a pencil where it was, and mark again ten minutes later. Then ask yourself what else is moving right now without our noticing. The answer is not part of the course.
city.xtx.science_spoon.title: Physics with One Spoon (experiments for the kitchen table)
city.xtx.sea_tides.1: Visitors ask when our tide comes in. We answer that ours is polite and arrives by two or three centimetres. The Baltic is almost closed on every side; the moon tugs at it like a clumsy guest at a tablecloth, and the water merely wrinkles a little. So our sand does not run out for a kilometre as in Normandy, but lies still, and children know where the shore ends better than any map.
city.xtx.sea_tides.2: So what changes the level? The wind. A westerly drives the water to our shore like a shepherd driving a flock, and then at the pier the water stands a palm or two above the lowest mark. An easterly leads it away, and the piles show the dark sides that are usually hidden. Old fishermen look not at the calendar but at the piles. "The water has gone by itself, expect the west," they say, and are usually right.
city.xtx.sea_tides.3: There are also seiches: after a storm the sea rocks back and forth like water in a basin that has been carried and set down. It rocks for an hour, sometimes for a day, and the quiet people on the pier speak in half-voices as if afraid to wake it. On the last page is a table of water levels for the year, and above it, in the librarian's hand: "Don't trust the numbers, go and look. Only take a scarf." And I did, honestly, take a scarf.
city.xtx.sea_tides.title: Why the Baltic Has No Tides (and What It Has Instead)
city.xtx.store_complaints.1: Entry one, in red pencil. "I complain about the staircase. It leads to the second floor, and I wanted the third, and now I am forced to think. Respectfully, a customer who did not get through." The manager's reply in the margin, green pen: "We have no third floor. It is not the staircase's fault but your dream's. A commendable dream, though: we have passed it to the architect. Come back and we'll think together."
city.xtx.store_complaints.2: Entry, middle of the page. "I suggest hanging a notice by the entrance: 'Umbrellas found in the departments are not to wander.' The yellow one with the duck head is out again, and I have been in the queue for it for the third day. Signed: Lidiya Sergeyevna." Reply: "The notice has been hung, but the umbrella does not read our language. Please wait by the lost and found: it likes to return to where it is expected. The watchman has been told not to interfere."
city.xtx.store_complaints.3: Entry, nearer the end, in a child's hand. "I want to complain about the little train. It goes round and round and doesn't take me to the station. Please take me. I am six. Boris." Reply in an adult hand, neatly: "Dear Boris, the station called 'Station' is under repair, but the little train promises to take you there on Monday. Please bring a passenger with you, preferably a plush one. No ticket is needed, only faith. Yours, the department store."
city.xtx.store_complaints.4: The last entry, without complaints. "Thank you. Not for the goods (I bought nothing), but for the fact that in this building you can stand an hour by a window and nobody asks what you want. I only want it always to be so. This is a suggestion. No signature." The manager replied below, in a slightly shaking hand: "Accepted. We will try. Come in on Thursday: there will be a fresh page and a new pencil. And this is for you." A little sweet is pinned to the page.
city.xtx.store_complaints.title: The Department Store's Book of Complaints and Suggestions (the visitors' copy)
city.xtx.store_pattern_raincoat.1: This raincoat is sewn in an evening and worn for three years. Use a Bologna-type raincoat fabric, preferably a light one: at dusk the child can be seen from far away. You need two metres of cloth, a zip or five buttons, thread to match and a little patience. The pattern is simple: two rectangles for the back and fronts, two for the sleeves, one for the hood. All measurements are on the next page, and here is the secret: cut generously, because children grow at night.
city.xtx.store_pattern_raincoat.2: Measurements for a height of 110 cm. Back: 40 by 55. Fronts: 22 by 55 each. Sleeve: 36 by 28, with 6 cm extra for the cuff, which is let down later. Hood: 28 by 34, fold in half and sew along the back of the head. Turn up the hem wide, a hand's breadth: in a year let down the hem and the coat will be longer without a sewing machine. Press the seams from the wrong side through a damp cloth, and very quietly, because an iron, like a child, dislikes hurry.
city.xtx.store_pattern_raincoat.3: A last piece of advice. Sew a small scrap of a different colour inside, by the collar, so that the coat knows its owner. There is no need to embroider a name on the scrap: the child knows whose coat it is. And on the hood you can sew a mushroom button, like the child's raincoat on the lowest rail in our department. It stands there with the tag "For those who grow faster than we sew". We ourselves can't keep up, by the way. That is why we print this leaflet.
city.xtx.store_pattern_raincoat.title: A Leaflet for Home Seamstresses: a Hooded Raincoat That Grows
city.xtx.store_radio_catalogue.1: "VOLNA-M" (Wave-M). A table set in a wooden case, three bands, an illuminated dial. Volume and tuning for different hands: the left for reception, the right for conscience. Picks up Lyudmilovsk radio well and falls dead silent when an electric razor is switched on next door. The salesman reminds you: the Volna dislikes being moved. Put it down once and that's enough; it will remember the place and be grateful.
city.xtx.store_radio_catalogue.2: "BEREG-4" (Shore-4). Portable, battery powered, with a strap and a telescopic aerial. Recommended for fishermen, shepherds and those who like to hear the weather forecast before it is told to them. Leather case included. Weight one kilogram two hundred grams, but at the end of the pier it feels lighter. A note in the saleswoman's hand: "Bought by two fishermen on a bet: who could catch Riga farther out. Both did. A third lost the bet."
city.xtx.store_radio_catalogue.3: "EFIR-60" (Ether-60). For those ready to listen at night. Short wave, fine tuning, earphones included: all in earnest. From the notes: "Recommended by the radio amateurs of Rassvet. The left earphone squeaks, but that's character." If you suddenly hear a voice that has no business on the air, don't hurry to switch off. The salesman says: "Listen to the end first. Then switch off. That is the order in which everything happens."
city.xtx.store_radio_catalogue.title: Catalogue of Radio Sets (household appliances, autumn issue)
city.xtx.sun_eight_minutes.1: Light takes a little over eight minutes to reach us from the Sun. So when you look at it (better not to look, but to look at what it lights up), you see it as it was eight minutes ago. For us that is almost nothing. But think: everything we see arrives slightly late. We live a little in the past, and nobody complains. Because the past, it turns out, is quite warm.
city.xtx.sun_eight_minutes.2: About the day. Our latitude is generous in summer and stingy in winter. In June it is light for almost eighteen hours and there is no night at all, only a long blue evening that turns into morning without apologising. In December the day is a little over six hours, and the sun walks low, like a person carrying a heavy bag. In those weeks the people of the upper terrace put the kettle by the window so that when the light comes it finds it boiling.
city.xtx.sun_eight_minutes.3: About spots. Sometimes dark spots appear on the Sun, each as big as several Earths, and cool by the Sun's standards: only four thousand degrees. They come and go in an eleven-year rhythm, and the astronomers of our town have kept a log of them since long ago. We have no observatory, but we do have smoked glass and patient people on a rooftop. The last entry in the log: "There is a spot. A small one. Don't worry, it is needed by somebody too."
city.xtx.sun_eight_minutes.4: The last page has no numbers. "If you have read this far, go outside and find where the sun is now. Not in the sky, because it hides in the clouds, but wherever it has done something: warmed a stone, dried the washing, warmed a cheek. That is its work, and it does it every day for everyone without asking for thanks. Say thank you, at least aloud. We have tested it: awkward, but it works."
city.xtx.sun_eight_minutes.title: The Sun: Eight Minutes Ago
city.xtx.t3_potter_notebook.1: Rule one: clay is always right until you have learned to argue with it. Take a lump the size of a loaf, knead it like dough to drive the bubbles out. A bubble in the clay means an explosion in the kiln, so we knead longer. Then onto the wheel: centre it. Clay is like character. Press too hard and it runs away; don't press and it won't stand. Hands wet, elbows against the thighs, eyes on the middle. When the centre is found you'll feel it: the wheel stops making noise.
city.xtx.t3_potter_notebook.3: Glaze recipes in two lines, because the rest is not a recipe but a matter of taste. Green: a shelf of glass, a pinch of copper and hope. Blue: the same, but cobalt and more hope. The jar marked "do not touch": add nothing and don't look. It will decide for itself what colour to come out. Whatever turns out better than planned I write on the back of the sheet, under the date. Whatever turns out worse, too. The back of this sheet is crowded now.
city.xtx.t3_potter_notebook.p2_1: Monday–Tuesday. The wheel. Bowl No. 7: centring, walls, rim. The walls are a bit thick at first, then thinner, then too thin, and that is a lesson too. We correct with a finger inside, the palm outside, the breath even. Cut off with wire and put on the shelf to dry. The bowl came out with one side higher than the other. "It's not a flaw," I told myself. "It's character." Then said it again, for conviction.
city.xtx.t3_potter_notebook.p2_2: Wednesday. The bowls stand on the shelf, drying: they pale like bread. They must not be touched: with a finger you can leave yourself in them for ever. Today we load the kiln for the first firing. Eight bowls, No. 7 among them, slightly lopsided but good. The kiln hums evenly, an orange light in the peephole. Look in no more than three times: that is my rule, and I break it four.
city.xtx.t3_potter_notebook.p2_3: Thursday. The kiln has cooled, the door ajar, and inside the bowls are pink and ringing: flick one with a nail and it sings. No. 7 is whole. No. 3 has cracked, and I have left it "for beauty": the crack runs like a river on a map. Today is glazing. Green, blue and the jar marked "do not touch", the most beautiful. In the jar the glaze is one colour, out of the kiln it will be another. Like people. I dipped No. 7 in the green and touched the bottom a little with blue.
city.xtx.t3_potter_notebook.p2_4: Friday. The second firing, with glaze, one thousand and sixty degrees. A red peephole, a quiet hum, a number in chalk on the kiln. Wet-looking but matt, the bowls stand in the kiln and know nothing of what awaits them. What I like in this work is precisely this: you lock what you have made into the fire and go home. And in the morning it is already different, and it is good if it is better. Today it will be better. I have decided so.
city.xtx.t3_potter_notebook.p2_5: Saturday. We opened the kiln. The finished ware shines like wet stones. No. 7 is green as the sea on a gloomy day, with two blue specks that I didn't paint. The kiln gave them. The bowl is slightly lopsided, and for that reason stands on the table more confidently than all the others. Beside it a slip: "Take them yourselves. If you can't take them, give them." I would give mine, but my hand won't rise yet. I'll give it on Sunday.
city.xtx.t3_potter_notebook.p2_6: Sunday. The kiln rests, like everyone. The shelf is empty, and on it stands a single bowl, somebody's, with a note: "This one is mine. Not to be given." Next to it a free place for mine. I put No. 7 there, then changed my mind and took it away. Then put it back. A potter must be able to give things away, but today is Sunday, and on Sunday everyone has a right to weakness. On Monday I begin a new one, and this I'll give to whoever will be happiest with it.
city.xtx.t3_potter_notebook.title: The Potter's Notebook: the Week of One Bowl
city.xtx.t3_timetable.1: TIMETABLE FOR THE WEEK. Monday, Wednesday, Friday, 15:00 to 19:00: basketball, boys ("Surf Juniors"). Tuesday and Thursday, same hours: gymnastics, girls, Lidiya Pavlovna's group. Saturday: weights before lunch, games after. Sunday: the hall is at your discretion, no coach, the ball is the responsibility of whoever took it. From 7 to 15 the hall is free; at 11:00 there is a PE lesson for class 6-B. The hall closes at 21:00.
city.xtx.t3_timetable.2: THE COACH'S NOTES. For newcomers: come not for a training session but for a habit. For the first week you may just watch. The second week, watch and run an easy lap along the wall. By the third week you are training, and I pretend I knew it all along. Sport doesn't like jerks, it likes those who come on a dull Tuesday. Stars are born on Wednesday, but only because on Tuesday somebody came.
city.xtx.t3_timetable.3: THE COACH'S NOTES (continued). On the ball: the ball is neither enemy nor friend, it is a conversation partner. Listen to it first, then answer. On shoes: street shoes come off at the door. We ask politely; the coach asks impolitely, but with love. On windows: the windows are dearer to me than the balls, and that is no joke, it is the budget. On opponents: the Seagulls play hard, which means fast, and fast is not frightening if you pass in time. On the extra lap: it is not a punishment, it is a conversation with yourself.
city.xtx.t3_timetable.title: The Sections' Timetable and the Coach's Notes
city.xtx.t3_tournament_rules.1: 1. A team: five players. The fifth may be a newcomer if he stands on the court and doesn't get in the way; this is compulsory. Substitutes sit on the bench and cheer in half-voices. 2. The game: two halves of ten minutes, with tea in between (the tea is paid for). 3. There is one referee, his decision is final, but discussion of it is permitted after the game. 4. Balls are brought onto the court only by the captains; the others watch.
city.xtx.t3_tournament_rules.2: 5. Points: two for a shot from under the basket, three from the far mark. A shot into your own basket goes in the record but not in the score and not as a reproach: errors on court happen to everybody, and to newcomers with special zeal. 6. The winner receives the "Golden Ball": it is, truth be told, wood painted gold, but very beautiful. Second place receives a certificate and the right to tell the whole yard about it. Third receives tea and applause.
city.xtx.t3_tournament_rules.3: 7. Spectators: places on the benches, don't catch the balls, catch the mood. Noise is permitted, but only for, not against. 8. If a team loses but plays beautifully, it is entitled to an extra round of applause. 9. If a team wins but plays ugly, it is entitled to one too, but quieter. 10. The last rule: the tournament exists so that afterwards the yard is a little closer together. Everything else is extra.
city.xtx.t3_tournament_rules.title: Rules of the Courtyards' Tournament "Golden Ball"
city.xtx.tarelka_guest_book.p2_1: Monday, 8:10. "I came before anyone else to have a coffee before the week began. The week had already begun, but they served the coffee anyway, thank you. In the case: the Potato cake and two éclairs. I took the Potato and promised myself not to think about the tests. I failed, but the Potato is delicious. — A teacher from the school on the second terrace."
city.xtx.tarelka_guest_book.p2_2: Tuesday. "I had the Napoleon. The layers are so thin that I counted and lost count at forty. The waitress said there are sixty-four and she didn't lie: checked with a fork. From the shipyard, lunch is fifteen minutes, but I'm twenty late. The boss will understand: I'm bringing him a slice. — Fitter, fifth grade."
city.xtx.tarelka_guest_book.p2_3: Wednesday. "Little baskets with a berry, and on each the berry sits exactly in the middle. My son (six) said that is what real seals look like, and ate the seal. Then he asked for another, just in case, to keep the papers in order. We shared the second. Thank you for the architecture and for the berry. — Dad and son."
city.xtx.tarelka_guest_book.p2_4: Thursday. "An apple puff pastry, and on the price tag, added by hand: 'last one, don't be shy'. I was shy. For a minute. Then I took it. The apple inside is warm, as if just taken out of someone's palm. I noticed the hall is quiet today: everyone is listening to the lighthouse in the window. — The lighthouse duty man, after his shift."
city.xtx.tarelka_guest_book.p2_5: Friday. "Anthill: a brown mound with nuts and not a single ant. I checked: at our age you check. My friend took the same, because 'I can't trust you with it alone'. We sat for two hours and not once talked about business. We walked home slowly, with a little box. I leave this entry so that I can later check whether it really was so. — Two friends."
city.xtx.tarelka_guest_book.p2_6: Saturday. "We took the whole Saucer cake for tea: round, glazed, with a wafer on top like a staircase. Six of us cut it, and each got exactly enough to want more. Grandmother said this is called 'culture of consumption'. The parrot announced the next stop and we all laughed. — Six people, three generations."
city.xtx.tarelka_guest_book.p2_7: Sunday. "Pastries on a tray with a red rim, and a sign: 'Take one each. In exceptional cases, two.' I decided my case was exceptional. Then I looked at the queue behind me and understood that everybody's case is exceptional. I took one. It turned out to be the kind that made me exceptional. — A reader of this book."
city.xtx.tarelka_guest_book.p4_1: A morning entry, in the barista's hand. "If you are reading this in the morning, you are one of those who see the light go on at the lighthouse. Not at sunset but at dawn, when the lamp is still burning but already shy. I stand at the window with my first cup and think that all days should be like this: someone quietly going out as another light rises. Come tomorrow, we'll do it again."
city.xtx.tarelka_guest_book.p4_2: An evening entry, in a stranger's hand, written in haste. "It is good to be silent here. You come in from the street, sit by the window, and the town below slowly lights its lamps one by one, and you owe no one anything. I came to write about work and wrote this instead. The book took it. Thank you. I'll finish the work at home." Beside it, in a round hand: "We know. Come again."
city.xtx.tarelka_guest_book.title: The Guest Book of the Saucer Café
city.xtx.tarelka_menu.1: DRINKS AND THE REST. Coffee 30. Tea 15. Tarragon soda 18. Water 20. Ice cream 30. Pie 18. Biscuits 20. At the bottom in chalk: "We serve coffee with a saucer, because we are the Saucer and must. If you ask for 'the usual', the barista already knows which. If you are here for the first time, ask for 'the usual' and see what happens. Usually it turns out well."
city.xtx.tarelka_menu.4: Below, in small print. "A request to guests: don't feed the parrot anything but sunflower seeds, and only if you said 'Terminus'. There is one telescope by the window, so take turns, without arguments. The jukebox takes a coin, not a button. Return saucers to the bar; they remember where they came from. If something displeased you, tell us, not the door. Our door is a revolving one and takes everything personally."
city.xtx.tarelka_menu.p2_1: DISH OF THE DAY. Monday: noodle soup. Grandmother's recipe; don't ask grandmother. The noodles are thin, the broth clear, and on top dill that the cook adds without looking, and therefore always exactly enough. Noodles come with a slice of bread. Our bread is from the lower terrace, where they bake from four in the morning, and the crust sometimes has flour on it like frost.
city.xtx.tarelka_menu.p2_2: DISH OF THE DAY. Tuesday: cutlets with mashed potato. The cook makes the mash himself, doesn't spare the butter, and asks dieticians not to look. The cutlets are golden and juicy, served hot: if they have gone cold, you got to talking, which is a compliment to the company. With them a home-pickled cucumber with garlic and a blackcurrant leaf; don't ask where the leaf comes from. From where it should.
city.xtx.tarelka_menu.p2_3: DISH OF THE DAY. Wednesday: fish with potatoes. The fish was brought from the pier in the morning and was still arguing. It is fried whole or in pieces, as the cook decides by the fish and his mood. The potatoes are boiled, with butter, herbs and a word of honour. The lemon comes on a saucer but squeezing it is optional: many simply look at the lemon and calm down.
city.xtx.tarelka_menu.p2_4: DISH OF THE DAY. Thursday: stuffed cabbage. Today probably the best in the district, tomorrow merely good: the cook is honest about it. The cabbage leaf is tender, the filling meat and rice, the sauce tomato and slightly sweet. Served with sour cream, and our sour cream is the kind that makes you want to add a spoon to your tea. Don't: the tea will be offended.
city.xtx.tarelka_menu.p2_5: DISH OF THE DAY. Friday: syrniki, curd fritters. With sour cream, but he who remembers the sour cream is the one who takes it. Golden, soft inside, with a vanilla smell that travels through the hall before the waitress does. Served three to a plate, and it would be good to stop at three: a fourth will also appear, but for it you will have to sit longer. Which is, after all, the main point of a café.
city.xtx.tarelka_menu.p2_6: DISH OF THE DAY. Saturday: plov for everyone. Whoever came earlier gets the bit from the bottom: that is the tastiest, the crust, with a head of garlic in the middle. It is served as one big shared mound, and it must be divided fairly. That is probably the best way to get to know a person: by whom he pushes the plate toward. The cook claims it works for him as a test. Those who pass come again.
city.xtx.tarelka_menu.p2_7: DISH OF THE DAY. Sunday: the cook does not cook. He only warms up what is left from Saturday and calls it home cooking. What exactly is left depends on how Saturday went. If it went well, little is left. If splendidly, nothing at all, and then he makes fried eggs, which are also homemade. Sunday at the Saucer is the day when everything is allowed except hurrying.
city.xtx.tarelka_menu.title: Menu of the Saucer Café (a card with a bent corner)
city.xtx.travel_terraces.1: Morning. Don't be late for the first cabin: it is empty, and the view from it belongs to you alone. Don't ride straight to the top, but station by station: on every terrace the town is different, and this is the only guide in which the sight is the ascent itself. Take a bread roll and don't be afraid of the gulls: they pretend not to be interested, and that is exactly why they are so close.
city.xtx.travel_terraces.2: Afternoon. Walk down to the lighthouse along the promenade and go to the end of the pier: there you will understand why people come here. Lunch is best at the Saucer: the café looks like a saucer, and in a saucer, as everyone knows, there is always room for one more cup. If a parrot sits at the bar announcing the next stop, don't be surprised and answer "Terminus": he likes to be answered. On market days everything is a little cheaper and the conversations a little longer.
city.xtx.travel_terraces.3: Evening. The last cabin goes up to the top terrace half an hour before sunset. Don't be lazy, go up: from the platform by the sanatorium you can watch the sun sink behind the farthest roof, and for a minute the whole town turns one colour. People below fall silent at that moment without knowing why. Don't break it. Then you can sit on a bench and wait for the first lamp. The lamps here come on one by one, and each seems like somebody's private request.
city.xtx.travel_terraces.title: Lyudmilovsk in One Day: a Visitor's Guide

quest.cafe_guest.desc: Leafing through the guest book by the stairs in the Saucer, I realised the pages are running out and my entry is not there.
quest.cafe_guest.done: Done. The barista, passing, glanced over my shoulder and nodded: "Now you're one of ours."
quest.cafe_guest.sign.log: The pen is right there. If I have no thoughts, I can draw a saucer.
quest.cafe_guest.sign.obj: Write an entry in the guest book
quest.cafe_guest.title: A page in the guest book
quest.cafe_kefir.bring.log: The bottle is in my pocket. I'll go to the kitchen hatch and tell the cook I've brought it.
quest.cafe_kefir.bring.obj: Hand the kefir to the cook
quest.cafe_kefir.buy.log: Kefir is sold at the department store, in the grocery section. I'll buy a bottle and come back to the kitchen hatch.
quest.cafe_kefir.desc: The cook at the Saucer has no sour cream today and pretends it doesn't matter. His plan B is kefir, and there's nobody to fetch it.
quest.cafe_kefir.done: The cook didn't turn round, but the pie was hot. So everything was done right.
quest.cafe_kefir.title: Kefir for the cook
quest.cafe_kesha.desc: A sheet under the menu says Kesha the parrot has come back on his own. He likes sunflower seeds and the word "Terminus". Worth checking.
quest.cafe_kesha.done: A pastry on the house. Kesha announced the last stop aloud, and then I thought he added "See you soon".
quest.cafe_kesha.feed.log: Kesha is watching me with one eye. The saucer says: first "Terminus", then the seeds.
quest.cafe_kesha.perch.log: Seeds in my pocket. I'll go to the perch at the end of the bar in the Saucer and take a look at Kesha.
quest.cafe_kesha.perch.obj: Talk to Kesha on his perch by the bar
quest.cafe_kesha.seeds.log: I need sunflower seeds. They say you can buy them at the market.
quest.cafe_kesha.title: Terminus
quest.capsule_cassette.back.log: I have the cassette. Nora didn't lose it, she forgot it: it must go to her recorder.
quest.capsule_cassette.back.obj: Listen to the cassettes at Nora's recorder
quest.capsule_cassette.cassette.log: The cassette lies on the bench of the seventh-floor bridge. The lift goes there.
quest.capsule_cassette.cassette.obj: Find the cassette on the seventh-floor bridge
quest.capsule_cassette.desc: A notice by the letter boxes says a cassette labelled Sea. Side B was found on the seventh-floor bridge. Nora in the capsule by the entrance must be missing it.
quest.capsule_cassette.done: The cassette went back into place, and the sound of surf came from the speaker, even as breathing. When Nora came back she listened in silence for a while, then said: "Now I know what question fourteen sounds like." She filled a whole bag with biscuits for me; less would have gone on the exam.
quest.capsule_cassette.notice.log: They're looking for the cassette's owner. The notice hangs by the boxes.
quest.capsule_cassette.notice.obj: Read the notices on the board by the letter boxes
quest.capsule_cassette.title: The cassette with the sea
quest.capsule_reel.back.log: I have the box. Ilmar sits over his recorder; let him hear what is on it.
quest.capsule_reel.back.obj: Listen to the tapes at Ilmar's recorder
quest.capsule_reel.desc: A notice by the letter boxes says a box with a reel of magnetic tape was found on the seventh-floor bridge. A lift at the end of the passage goes up there.
quest.capsule_reel.done: Ilmar put the reel on his recorder and the walls of the room went away: a far night voice read a forecast and then gave a call sign nobody had heard in forty years. "That was me," said Ilmar. "In my first year." He poured me tea and straightened the cup on its saucer twice.
quest.capsule_reel.notice.log: They're looking for the tape's owner. The notice hangs by the boxes.
quest.capsule_reel.notice.obj: Read the notices on the board by the letter boxes
quest.capsule_reel.reel.log: The box lies on the bench of the seventh-floor bridge. The lift goes there.
quest.capsule_reel.reel.obj: Find the box of tape on the seventh-floor bridge
quest.capsule_reel.title: The tape on the bridge
quest.checkup.desc: At the clinic they looked at me as if I'd been due for a check-up for ages. Well, if they've been waiting.
quest.checkup.doctor.log: Only the doctor left. He sees patients on weekdays until five.
quest.checkup.done: "Practically healthy," they wrote on my card. The nurse gave me a boiled sweet as if I were little. I didn't refuse.
quest.checkup.nurse.log: The nurse told me to step on the scales and read the eye chart. Then the doctor.
quest.checkup.title: Practically healthy
quest.chess_ladder.desc: In the club a ladder of names is chalked on a board. The bottom line is empty, and for some reason I feel awkward walking past it.
quest.chess_ladder.done: I wrote my name on the empty line. In chalk, small, so it can be rubbed out. Lev Markovich read it and nodded: that is how everybody starts.
quest.chess_ladder.play.log: Now I can sit down at a board. If I lose they will pour me tea; that's the custom here.
quest.chess_ladder.play.obj: Play a game of chess at the Rassvet
quest.chess_ladder.read.log: Before sitting down at a board I'll check the shelf: there should be a book of openings.
quest.chess_ladder.title: A rung of the ladder
quest.cinema_night.desc: They're showing a film at the Rassvet. The poster promises everyone cries at the end, even the projectionist.
quest.cinema_night.done: I came out of the cinema and the light outside had changed. For five minutes the town seemed like the film carrying on.
quest.cinema_night.film.log: A ticket is thirty roubles; the show runs while the projectionist is in, from three till late. I'll sit wherever I like.
quest.cinema_night.title: The evening show
quest.cinema_night.watch.obj: Watch a film at the Rassvet
quest.city_tour.desc: The town is big and I don't know anyone in it. I'll start by just walking through the main doors.
quest.city_tour.done: I've been round the whole centre. Every door greeted me as if I'd been there before.
quest.city_tour.see_cafe.obj: Go up to the Saucer café
quest.city_tour.see_club.obj: Look into the Rassvet culture house
quest.city_tour.title: The town by the sea
quest.city_tour.walk.log: The library, the department store, the market, the Rassvet, the clinic, the Saucer café. If I do something in each one, sit down, leaf through a book, buy something, maybe the town will remember me.
quest.clinic_card_book.book.log: Now open the card at the registry desk and see how it turned out.
quest.clinic_card_book.book.obj: Open the card on the registry desk
quest.clinic_card_book.desc: At the registry they start a card with five squares for stamps. A filled card, they say, can be prettier than a certificate.
quest.clinic_card_book.done: Five stamps: a drop, a giraffe, spectacles, the round violet one and the little man on the bars. The card came out nicer than a certificate. The registrar handed over two biscuits and tea: "For long service in the queue, and no snoring."
quest.clinic_card_book.first.log: The first two stamps: have my chest listened to at the therapist's and stand against the giraffe at the children's doctor's.
quest.clinic_card_book.growth.obj: Stand against the giraffe at the children's doctor's
quest.clinic_card_book.listen.obj: Have my chest listened to by the therapist
quest.clinic_card_book.second.log: Two more: show the vaccination card to the nurse by the cooler and exercise at the wall bars.
quest.clinic_card_book.title: A card full of stamps
quest.clinic_card_book.vaccine.obj: Show the vaccination card to the nurse
quest.clinic_fish.bottle.log: I have to bring my own water for the aquarium. The pharmacy window sells water.
quest.clinic_fish.desc: A single fish lives in the clinic, and the children call it the Head Doctor. They say it is lonely.
quest.clinic_fish.done: The jar clinked. The nurse nodded and pressed a few roubles into my hand for the fare: "Not for the money, for the care." The Head Doctor, I think, swam by a little more briskly.
quest.clinic_fish.jar.log: Only the jar on the reception desk is left: drop a coin in.
quest.clinic_fish.jar.obj: Drop a coin in the jar
quest.clinic_fish.notice.log: A note about the fish hangs on the board in the hall. I should read what they ask.
quest.clinic_fish.pour.log: The watering can is beside the aquarium. Time to top up the water.
quest.clinic_fish.read.obj: Read the note on the board
quest.clinic_fish.title: A friend for the Head Doctor
quest.clinic_sharp.ball.log: Third exam in the hall by the wall bars: four times in a row, don't drop the medicine ball.
quest.clinic_sharp.ball.obj: Don't drop the ball by the wall bars
quest.clinic_sharp.desc: The clinic has a chart, a ruler and a medicine ball: three tiny exams for anyone who wants them. They say whoever passes all three is entered in the "healthy team".
quest.clinic_sharp.done: All three exams passed. They didn't put me on a "healthy team": there's no such team. But the nurse gave me two sweets and shook my hand like a colleague.
quest.clinic_sharp.eyes.log: First exam at the eye doctor's: read the chart by the pointer down to the smallest row.
quest.clinic_sharp.eyes.obj: Read the chart to the smallest row
quest.clinic_sharp.reflex.log: Second exam in the children's doctor's room: catch the falling ruler.
quest.clinic_sharp.reflex.obj: Catch the ruler at the children's doctor's
quest.clinic_sharp.title: Three little exams
quest.clinic_ticket.desc: There is a squared-up chair by the door of Room 4. Nobody sits on it. I wonder why.
quest.clinic_ticket.done: A plate like any plate. But when the instruments clinked behind the door I wanted to move seats. I console myself that my blood pressure is an astronaut's.
quest.clinic_ticket.door.log: Now I can stand by the dentist's door and read the plate. Just read it.
quest.clinic_ticket.door.obj: Read the plate on the door of Room 4
quest.clinic_ticket.height.obj: Measure my height at the wall
quest.clinic_ticket.prep.log: Before going near that door I should get myself in order: have the nurse take my height and blood pressure.
quest.clinic_ticket.title: A ticket to the dentist
quest.cog_clock.desc: The Cog club's chess clock has gone missing. Everyone seems to know it's gone and nobody knows where.
quest.cog_clock.done: The buffet lady brought tea and a biscuit "for the return". She said the clock came back the most proper way: by itself. I didn't argue.
quest.cog_clock.find.log: Something ticks upstairs. Grasshoppers don't live indoors, but circles do.
quest.cog_clock.look.log: I'll start with the notices: the club's boards usually say more than whoever wrote them meant to.
quest.cog_clock.notices.obj: Read the notices on the club's boards
quest.cog_clock.place.obj: Put the clock back on the chess table
quest.cog_clock.set.log: Seryozha asked me to take the clock back so he wouldn't have to explain. I'll put it in its place and nobody will have to explain anything.
quest.cog_clock.title: The cracked clock
quest.cog_reader.cart.log: Last, a look at the returns trolley: you can see who read what, which is almost like meeting them.
quest.cog_reader.desc: The club library doesn't lend books to just anyone, but the magazines go round freely. I'll start at the shelves.
quest.cog_reader.done: Tamara Ilyinichna stamped "Cog Club. Library" on a postcard and said I was a reader now. The stamp came out crooked, but it's real.
quest.cog_reader.look.obj: See what has been returned to the trolley
quest.cog_reader.read.log: Chess, engineering, the sea. In the margins of every book someone has already argued with the author.
quest.cog_reader.swap.log: By the end wall there is a swap rack: bring one, take one. I have nothing yet, but they let you take a magazine anyway.
quest.cog_reader.take.obj: Take a magazine from the swap rack
quest.cog_reader.title: A reader at the club
quest.commune_cat.board.log: The committee board by the entrance. I'll read the news about the cat.
quest.commune_cat.desc: The house committee board asks people not to feed Markiz the cat and to report where he was seen. He has been seen everywhere.
quest.commune_cat.done: Markiz came to the film, sat on the committee's bench and watched to the end. I got the place beside him. The committee poured tea for us both, his in a saucer.
quest.commune_cat.evening.log: The committee invites everyone to the television evening, Markiz too. I'll sit near him.
quest.commune_cat.fold_laundry.obj: Sort the laundry on the table by the washers
quest.commune_cat.lost_box.obj: Look in the lost-property box by the door
quest.commune_cat.read_board.obj: Read the house committee board in the hall
quest.commune_cat.search.log: They say the cat likes things warm and soft. I'll check the basket by the folding table and the lost-property box.
quest.commune_cat.title: The cat in the sailor vest
quest.commune_cat.watch_tv.obj: Watch the television in the hall
quest.commune_charter.bench.log: The bench by the entrance, under the committee's board. I'll sit and read the charter to the end.
quest.commune_charter.desc: The house charter lies by the committee's bench, with an empty space at the bottom: amendments are brought by whoever sits and thinks aloud. I'll try.
quest.commune_charter.done: I never came up with an amendment, but I understood what the house stands on: the bench, the dominoes, the shared mug. Lidiya Arkadyevna said, "Enough for a first time," and gave me a pie.
quest.commune_charter.game.log: The charter says: "A dispute is settled at the table, not behind the door." The dominoes table is by the wall bars.
quest.commune_charter.read_charter.obj: Read the house charter on the committee's bench
quest.commune_charter.tea.log: After the game comes tea. The samovar is by the wall, the mug on its chain.
quest.commune_charter.title: An amendment to the charter
quest.commune_cloud.board.log: The committee board by the entrance has a sheet for every day. I'll read what it says today.
quest.commune_cloud.desc: By the door of the commune house hall hangs the house committee's report about a leak. I'd like to know how it all ended.
quest.commune_cloud.done: After the programme Lidiya Arkadyevna led everyone to see the little cloud on the ceiling in 1-05, with a kettle instead of a pointer. They poured me tea: viewers are entitled to it, they said.
quest.commune_cloud.evening.log: The committee calls everyone to the television evening. I'll take a seat close to the screen.
quest.commune_cloud.gossip.log: The surest news is found at the chess board and in the wall newspaper. I'll look in at both.
quest.commune_cloud.play_chess.obj: Sit down with the chess players by the wall
quest.commune_cloud.read_board.obj: Read the house committee board in the hall
quest.commune_cloud.title: A cloud on the ceiling
quest.commune_cloud.watch_tv.obj: Watch the television in the hall
quest.fair_prize_run.board.log: First I'll find out what is being drawn today: the programme hangs on the board with the posters.
quest.fair_prize_run.board.obj: Read the fair's programme on the poster board
quest.fair_prize_run.desc: On the tiered stand by the ring toss stands a clockwork duck and everybody looks at it. I want to win her fairly: with the programme, a ticket and a throw.
quest.fair_prize_run.done: The duck wound up and waddled along the counter. The seller said: "See? She has remembered you."
quest.fair_prize_run.look.obj: Go to the prize stand by the ring toss
quest.fair_prize_run.lot.obj: Draw a ticket in the lottery
quest.fair_prize_run.ring.log: Ring toss: three throws. I need to land them so that the seller sighs.
quest.fair_prize_run.shelf.log: All that's left is to go to the tiered stand and look at the duck up close.
quest.fair_prize_run.ticket.log: The lottery is the fairest way to warm up: a ticket, the drum, a postcard.
quest.fair_prize_run.title: The duck from the fair
quest.fair_record.desc: At the fair's strongman gauge hangs a plaque with somebody's record. A tripod stands next to it. I want to leave a mark too.
quest.fair_record.done: A new print in my diary: me at the gauge, the bell overhead, my eyes just above the record number. The photographer signed the back and added, "Third place is waiting."
quest.fair_record.hit.log: Now the mallet. Two roubles is cheap for the right to ring the bell.
quest.fair_record.photo.log: The photographer promised to shoot those who hit the gauge. I'll go to the tripod.
quest.fair_record.pose.obj: Have my photo taken at the tripod
quest.fair_record.read.obj: Read the record plaque by the strongman gauge
quest.fair_record.record.log: First I'll read the plaque: I need to know which number to reach for.
quest.fair_record.title: A record at the bell
quest.fair_sandal.basket.log: The Lost and Found basket stands by the chair scales. I'll take it there.
quest.fair_sandal.desc: On the fair's notice board hangs a note about a child's sandal. The left one is looking for the right one. Or the other way round.
quest.fair_sandal.done: The pair met. They say that at that moment somewhere at the fair a girl in one sandal stopped limping.
quest.fair_sandal.find.log: The thing to do is look under a bench. Fine, I'll look under a bench.
quest.fair_sandal.fortune.log: The fortune-telling automaton talks about lost things. I'll ask it, just in case.
quest.fair_sandal.look.obj: Find the sandal under a bench among the kiosks
quest.fair_sandal.notice.log: First I'll read the notice on the board, in case there are details.
quest.fair_sandal.put.obj: Put the sandal in the Lost and Found basket by the scales
quest.fair_sandal.read.obj: Read the notices on the fair's board
quest.fair_sandal.title: A sandal under the bench
quest.first_chess.desc: At the Cog club there are people at the chess tables who never seem to get up.
quest.first_chess.done: After the game the buffet lady brought me tea "for bravery". She said losers always get a glass here.
quest.first_chess.game.log: I'll sit at a free board. Someone is bound to join me; that's the custom here.
quest.first_chess.play.obj: Play a game of chess at the Cog club
quest.first_chess.title: First game
quest.hall_audition.ask.log: The play has one line about the choir, and Isla's choir is twenty-two people. The choir leader rehearses on the stage from five to nine, Wednesday to Sunday. I will ask about an audition.
quest.hall_audition.ask.obj: Ask the choir leader about the audition
quest.hall_audition.board.log: The caretaker said that the stubs of the evenings are hung on the board in the foyer. Time to hang mine: I will look at the nail marked "Choir".
quest.hall_audition.board.obj: Look at the stub board in the foyer
quest.hall_audition.desc: On a table in the lobby of the Vaults lie programmes. One says the «Surf» choir takes new people, though not everyone, and that in the play the choir plays the clocks. I wonder how.
quest.hall_audition.done: The "Choir" stub hangs on its nail, red and a little crumpled. The echo in the hall caught my last note and gave it back to me, a little lower. So we have an understanding.
quest.hall_audition.script.log: In the play the choir is the clocks backstage. The prompter's copy lies on the stand by the left wing. I will see what it says about the choir.
quest.hall_audition.script.obj: Read the play on the prompter's stand backstage
quest.hall_audition.title: A voice trial
quest.hall_audition.trial.log: I have to stand on the chalk cross at the front of the stage and sing so that Isla nods. Clean, loud or with feeling: she judges by what I choose in answer to her face.
quest.hall_audition.trial.obj: Win a voice trial with the choir leader
quest.hall_dance_night.book.log: After the dancing it is the custom to write one's impressions in the guest book in the foyer. Almost a compulsory item of the programme.
quest.hall_dance_night.book.obj: Leave an entry in the guest book in the foyer
quest.hall_dance_night.desc: The poster in the lobby announces a dance night. Better not to stand by the wall but to step onto the floor. First, though, I must work out what is expected of me.
quest.hall_dance_night.done: I wrote: "Came in for a minute, stayed for a waltz." The caretaker nodded: that is exactly what everyone writes who comes again. And poured me some tea.
quest.hall_dance_night.floor.log: My feet seem to obey. Time to step onto the dance floor.
quest.hall_dance_night.mirror.log: First a rehearsal in front of the mirror: the side hall has a barre and a wall-sized mirror.
quest.hall_dance_night.mirror.obj: Stand at the barre mirror in the dance room
quest.hall_dance_night.title: Dancing at the Vaults
quest.hall_premiere.board.log: A notice from the Wave theatre is pinned by the entrance. I'll read what they have for today.
quest.hall_premiere.board.obj: Read the theatre's notice in the lobby
quest.hall_premiere.desc: In the Assembly Hall an amateur theatre is preparing the play Time, Forward! They say the club's chess clock was last seen somewhere other than the club. I'll look in; maybe I will be of use.
quest.hall_premiere.done: The echo clapped along with the hall, and the handyman-Clockmaker bowed as if he really had stopped time. At the door the caretaker pressed forty roubles into my hand: "For paying attention. Buy a pie at the buffet and tell the chess players about the clock."
quest.hall_premiere.props.log: They need a big clock and the club is looking for a small one. I'll look at the props table backstage: maybe the two will meet.
quest.hall_premiere.props.obj: Look over the props table backstage
quest.hall_premiere.show.log: All is ready. I'll take a seat in the hall and watch Time go forward.
quest.hall_premiere.show.obj: Watch the play from a seat in the hall
quest.hall_premiere.title: Premiere at the Vaults
quest.home_aoki.desc: The seamstress Rimma Aoki lives at the top of the second stepped house. The door is open; a clock ticks and fabric rustles in the draught.
quest.home_aoki.done: At the Rassvet the cashier heard me out and wrote in her book: "Sun: will be there." She gave me twenty-five roubles "for the tram". There are no trams in Lyudmilovsk. "Well, for the cable car, then," said the cashier.
quest.home_aoki.dress.log: Something almost finished under the machine's needle. I'll see what.
quest.home_aoki.dress.obj: Look at the sewing under the needle
quest.home_aoki.fitting.log: By her calendar, the costume fitting for the Rassvet is on Thursday, and the Sun for the play isn't ready. I'll look in at the Rassvet and tell them the Sun is being sewn and will be there.
quest.home_aoki.fitting.obj: Tell the cashier at the Rassvet's ticket window
quest.home_aoki.swatches.log: One sun on the hem isn't finished: she couldn't find the right yellow. There are swatches on the wall. Maybe I can find it.
quest.home_aoki.swatches.obj: Pick out a yellow among the swatches on the wall
quest.home_aoki.title: A sun for the hem
quest.home_bauer.desc: On the board in the middle hall of the serpent house there's a notice: Colette in no. 17 needs a piece of sea glass for her aquarium. Her door on the first-floor gallery is open from ten.
quest.home_bauer.dish.log: Glass in my pocket. Up the stairs in the left corner of the hall, then left along the gallery. Door 17.
quest.home_bauer.dish.obj: Put the glass on Colette's saucer in no. 17
quest.home_bauer.done: Colette held the glass to the window and said nothing for a long time. Then she put some biscuits in my hand: "The Pilot will be pleased. He is particular."
quest.home_bauer.glass.log: Sea glass turns up on the shore, especially after the waves. I should wander along the water's edge.
quest.home_bauer.glass.obj: Find a piece of sea glass on the shore
quest.home_bauer.notice.log: The notice hangs on the board by the concierge. I should read all of it, there's something about the door and the hours.
quest.home_bauer.notice.obj: Read the notice on the board in the middle hall
quest.home_bauer.title: A piece of glass for the Pilot
quest.home_brandt.beds.log: Now to the roof: climb to level four, step onto the roof above flat 3-03 and water the tomatoes, the herbs and the sunflowers, each in its own way.
quest.home_brandt.desc: On the board by the stairs hangs a request from 3-03: Agata Brandt has a broken wrist, and on the roof above her flat grow tomatoes, herbs and sunflowers. The tap is on level two, the can is in the barrel on the roof, and Agata's door is open.
quest.home_brandt.done: Agata did not say thank you. She looked a long time at the wet soil, then at you, and said: "There. And I thought there was nobody." She poured tea and pushed an apple across: "Take it. It's from that very tree."
quest.home_brandt.herbs.obj: Water the herbs on the roof
quest.home_brandt.jar.log: On the shelf by the radio stands a jar labelled "Seeds that didn't leave". It was left for anyone who wants to plant something at home.
quest.home_brandt.jar.obj: Take seeds from the jar in flat 3-03
quest.home_brandt.notebook.log: Agata has left her seed notebook on the desk in her flat. You'd like to understand where these plants came from.
quest.home_brandt.notebook.obj: Read the seed notebook in flat 3-03
quest.home_brandt.sunflowers.obj: Water the sunflowers on the roof
quest.home_brandt.tap.log: First job: get some water. The tap stands by a window on level two, the bucket beside it. The stairs from entrance A lead right to it.
quest.home_brandt.tap.obj: Get water at the tap on level two
quest.home_brandt.title: Water for Agata
quest.home_brandt.tomatoes.obj: Water the tomatoes on the roof
quest.home_cube_a.desc: A notice on the deck's stand says the second cube needs a gardener for the weekend. The way in is the niche at the cube's foot with a tiny lift; upstairs Gennady keeps a greenhouse of peppers.
quest.home_cube_a.diary.log: The greenhouse diary lies by the bed; Gennady seems to expect it to be read.
quest.home_cube_a.done: Gennady came back from the lakes tanned and went straight up to the bed. Then he came down and silently set a jar of pepper jam before you. On the lid: "Careful: honestly hot."
quest.home_cube_a.note.log: The notes on the fridge of the second cube explain what to do. The lift is in the hall at the foot of the cube.
quest.home_cube_a.note.obj: Read the notes on the fridge in the cube
quest.home_cube_a.title: A greenhouse in the tip
quest.home_cube_a.water.log: The can is by the cactus, upstairs. A glass per pot, no more.
quest.home_cube_a.water.obj: Water the greenhouse in the tip
quest.home_cube_b.box.log: The X is the chest in the greenhouse corner. You may open it: Mette allowed it.
quest.home_cube_b.desc: Mette's map hangs on the fridge of the third cube. An X sits near the tip. The lift is in the niche at the cube's foot.
quest.home_cube_b.done: Mette solemnly handed you two sweets and a cookie. "Now you are on the team," she said. "The lift already knows you."
quest.home_cube_b.map.log: Mette drew the map on the fridge. First read it.
quest.home_cube_b.map.obj: Read the map on the fridge
quest.home_cube_b.shoes.obj: Look at the shoes in the hall
quest.home_cube_b.stars.log: The map names three landmarks: the shoes at the entrance, the toy bin and the seed trays in the tip.
